title: The Tension Between Two of the Democrats’ Biggest Promises
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
On Wednesday morning, Americans awoke to the news that the Democrats had retaken both the House and the Senate
The next day, the stock market hemorrhaged $2.5 trillion
Alphabet, Nvidia, and the major semiconductor companies shed billions

Tesla and SpaceX, whose founder, Elon Musk, had spent half a billion dollars trying to keep Democrats out of Congress, were suddenly worth approximately $420 billion less than they had been two days before
In some ways, the election results were a referendum on Big Tech

Recent polls have revealed that most voters want the government to impose new regulations on AI, and many victorious Democrats campaigned on a promise to move away from the unchecked expansionism that has defined the industry during the Donald Trump era

Texas Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-Elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina have both pledged to stop the construction of new data centers, which have been the subject of voter panic across the country in recent months. (These facilities—physical manifestations of the industry’s clout—can raise local electricity costs and pollute the air.) Others vowed to stand up to imperious Silicon Valley elites, or to hold the president accountable for his corruption—much of which is linked to his family’s cryptocurrency ventures
Last week’s sell-off was a sign that the stock market is taking lawmakers at their word
At the same time, the dip hinted at a potential challenge for Democrats
Voters made clear that they were unhappy with the cost of living, and many Democrats who ran on affordability ended up winning big
Widespread fears about what AI might do to jobs only fueled the party’s comeback

The irony is that AI companies are responsible for a sizable chunk of the United States’ GDP growth; AI products have invaded our professional and personal lives, as well as our pension funds and 401(k)s
All Americans now have a stake in the AI economy, whether they’ve opted in or not
It might even be more accurate to say that, at this point, AI is the economy

According to a recent Bloomberg story, “nearly $32 trillion in market value had been added to the S&P 500 Index since OpenAI released ChatGPT, and more than half of that gain came from just 10 companies—all linked to artificial intelligence.” The article also noted that “almost all the growth in US business spending last year came from spending on technology,” much of which is, of course, connected to AI and the ongoing data-center build-out
The technology’s effects on the economy are complex, and not purely positive: Demand for AI is contributing to inflation and helping keep long-term-bond yields relatively high
But AI has become so entrenched that Democrats’ efforts to target the industry could have ripple effects
Their challenge will be to regulate AI in the ways they campaigned on without damaging the economy they’ve promised to protect
It’s no accident that this technology has so thoroughly infiltrated the world of American business

Many companies have been eager to adopt it (despite the lack of proof that it makes workers more productive), and investors are hungry for a piece of what they see as humanity’s next great technical evolution
But the federal government has enabled this expansion too

Even though the industry’s leaders have warned that their technology may destroy the world, and even though AI’s ability to wreak havoc on vital infrastructure, such as banks and power grids, has become clearer and clearer, the Trump administration has refused to implement strict controls on the sector
In fact, the White House has gone out of its way to try to override state-level rule making on AI, asking Congress to adopt its pro-AI policy recommendations
And the president himself has maintained close relationships with Silicon Valley’s leaders and personally invested in AI firms

Recall that the CEOs of Meta, Apple, and Google stood behind Trump at his second inauguration, and that their companies collectively donated tens of millions of dollars to the new White House ballroom
Meanwhile, the administration’s other policies have weakened the economy
Although the stock market has done well during Trump’s second term, the health of the American economy is measured in more than just the valuations of its biggest companies
The president’s decision to implement tariffs and to start a war in Iran have pushed up the cost of living
Energy prices have spiked, and inflation has lately outpaced wage growth, meaning that workers’ dollars aren’t going as far
Now lawmakers have a chance to fight for the kind of changes they’ve been promising, and AI is an important part of their calculus

My colleague Matteo Wong wrote earlier this month that AI is an engine of growth, but it’s also hogging some of the attention and the investments that might have once gone to other sectors. “The industry seems to be holding not just the American economy but our entire society hostage,” he explained. “Nvidia, Google, and the like had better succeed financially, or there go your savings.” (Yesterday, Trump joined Silicon Valley leaders in defending Nvidia’s Jensen Huang after reports emerged that the CEO had cheated on his wife with an alleged Chinese spy—another acknowledgement of the country’s deep reliance on Huang and his company.) It doesn’t help that the Democrats don’t have a coherent plan for reining in AI

As my colleague Rogé Karma has written, individual candidates have proposed some ideas, including a federally controlled kill switch that can shut models down in an emergency and an outright pause on advanced AI development

Some have made the very reasonable point that slowing the growth of AI here in the United States is a moral imperative—a way to safeguard humanity, akin to nuclear disarmament—and that it’s more important than any economic trade-offs
But voters worried about their savings may not ultimately see it that way
There are geopolitical trade-offs, too: Although legislators can choose to hamper AI’s development in the U.S., it’s unlikely that China, the country’s primary tech rival, will choose to do the same
This week, the stock market has been well on the way to recovery
But if AI companies are weakened in the months and years to come, all Americans will eventually be affected—not just the early investors and executives stewarding this industry
Whatever congressional Democrats decide, the interconnectedness of the AI economy ensures that their moves will have consequences that extend well beyond their chosen targets
Related: America can’t afford an AI recession

title: Prepare for the AI Apocalypse Like You’d Prepare for a Snowstorm
excerpt: Since late last year, a small but growing chorus of cybersecurity experts has been warning that AI models were pushing the internet toward a sort of cataclysm
body: Since late last year, a small but growing chorus of cybersecurity experts has been warning that AI models were pushing the internet toward a sort of cataclysm
Hospitals, banks, utilities, basically anything and everything connected to the web could be hacked

Over the past month or so, those scenarios have come alive in almost spectacular fashion: Last month, AI was used to find major security flaws in software used by 70 percent of websites, prompting governments to take down their websites as a precaution
A week later, attackers targeted the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, in part by hijacking the company’s internal AI tools, and ultimately drained billions of dollars
This fall alone, AI has been used to hack hundreds of financial institutions in Latin America, not to mention data centers, banks, and government entities around the world
AI has also changed the economics of hacking, such that targeting individual people and small organizations is becoming cheap and easy enough to be worthwhile
And there’s a broader rise in cyberattacks that, though not directly tied to AI, likely leveraged the technology in some way

Last week, for instance, the FBI issued a warning about hacks targeting industrial refrigeration systems following attacks on grocery stores in France, Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Israel, and other countries. [ Read: Perhaps connecting fridges to the internet was a bad idea ] Governments and Silicon Valley entrepreneurs, who have been tracking this most closely, are steeling themselves against what promises to be an extended period of cybersecurity vulnerability—and they advise that you do the same
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently said that every U.S. military base should be able to continue operating even in the case of a cyberattack disrupting the power grid
Japan has declared a state of emergency in cyberspace
South Korea’s National Intelligence Service has reportedly ordered thousands of organizations to conduct emergency cybersecurity audits
The United Kingdom is telling citizens to have several days of water and food prepared in the event of a number of potential disasters, including a cyberattack
Everybody is starting to sound, just a little bit, like a doomsday prepper, and not without reason
So how do you keep your accounts, your family, and your finances all safe? For everyday users of the internet, there are low-lift steps you can take to avoid being a sitting duck in this new reality
The most important and easiest thing is to get your digital affairs in order
Use different passwords, ideally long and randomly generated, for all of your accounts and store them in a password manager
Enable two-factor authentication everywhere you can—that is, opt in to receiving a confirmation code on your phone or, ideally, inside a dedicated app to add a layer of security to sensitive accounts
In addition, frequently update laptops, smartphones, internet routers, and various applications

Otherwise, unpatched security flaws mean that clicking on a malicious link can allow a hacker to steal cookies and login information from your browser and bypass even two-factor authentication methods
But are they more annoying than having hackers dip into your life savings and post bitcoin advertisements from your X account ? No, they are not
Additionally, be extra wary of social engineering
Phishing scams have gotten really, really good: Fake customer-service websites now regularly turn up in search results and direct you to AI voice agents, ready to steal your private information
You may receive personalized texts that look like they’re from your boss, a real-estate agent, an IRS official—you name it
The first step in the historic hack on Binance reportedly started with an employee clicking on a malicious advertisement
So, be on guard and inspect links before clicking
That can be as simple as hovering your cursor over a hyperlink in your email to view the full website address to see if anything looks suspicious (misspellings, extra words and characters)
If a representative of your bank, power company, or another service provider calls you, double-check by calling them back on the official company number
If you start taking these basic steps to prepare for AI-powered cyberattacks, you might start wondering just how far you can go
In Silicon Valley, an industry flush with money and people who tend to envision all kinds of apocalyptic scenarios, many tend to go to extremes

The influential investor Peter Thiel, who has recently given lectures about the “Antichrist,” has a sprawling property in a remote part of New Zealand on which he once planned to build a bunker-like cottage before a local council rejected the proposal

In 2016, Sam Altman told The New Yorker that he has “guns, gold, potassium iodide, antibiotics, batteries, water, gas masks from the Israeli Defense Force, and a big patch of land in Big Sur I can fly to.” These are edge cases, but they can be instructive in their own ways
Others in Silicon Valley are undertaking less grandiose physical preparations

Jeffrey Ladish, the executive director of the AI-safety group Palisade Research, told me that he’s cautious about relying on the cloud to store his data. “It might be worth having a hard drive or some Blu-ray discs” with, say, photos and important documents

He also suggests stocking up at least a few days of food and clean water, as well as flashlights and some cash. “These could be useful whether it’s a pandemic, whether it’s a tornado, whether hacking takes down the power grid or takes down the banks,” he told me
Our conversation reminded him to check his supplies. “I should actually check on my fresh water,” he said

Edouard Harris, the chief technology officer of the AI-safety company Gladstone AI, recommended downloading “parts of the internet that you care about the most”—for me, that might mean saving the many Atlantic articles I’ve written that only exist online
If you’re the type who partakes in cryptocurrency, that could mean moving it to a “cold crypto wallet,” or an offline hard drive
On top of that, Harris told me, “my bank password, my core email-account password, things like that are just not saved in digital format
They’re just written down on paper.” He is worried about an AI-powered hack taking down crucial infrastructure, which could, for instance, limit his ability to get power or water
That’s not a far-fetched concern: This summer, cyberattacks disrupted water utilities across the country and shut down a British power plant

title: The Scapegals
excerpt: She’d been with President Trump since his first bid for the White House
body: She’d been with President Trump since his first bid for the White House
She was one of the few people who’d stuck around after the January 6 attacks on the U.S
Capitol, when just about everyone else thought his political career was over
And as his chief of staff for the past two years, she was a stabilizing force in an administration that sorely needed one
But Wiles—whom Trump jettisoned last week after Republicans’ devastating midterm losses—likely had at least one thing working against her: that second X chromosome

Since returning to the White House, Trump has refrained from the firing sprees of his first term, but he has shown a remarkable willingness to discard his female senior administration officials when they displease him
With the abrupt elevation of Stephen Miller to chief of staff last Friday, Wiles joined that most unenviable troop—The Scapegals

Including Wiles, Trump has fired or pushed out at least half a dozen top women this term, including Attorney General Pam Bondi, Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, and White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia. (Zacharia announced the departure of Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle from the White House podium—the only news she would share, it turned out—a mere three days before she, too, was summarily dismissed.) Other senior women have also left—Karoline Leavitt, who preceded Zacharia as press secretary, and Harmeet Dhillon, who ran the Civil Rights Division at the Justice Department, among others—albeit on their own terms
Most of the senior women who were forced out have since been replaced by men

When charges of misogyny pop up against Trump, as they have with regularity in both of his terms, his defenders are quick to claim that he is an equal-opportunity offender who is just as likely to attack, say, a white male journalist as he is a female reporter of color
But this time, counterexamples are hard to find

One of the few senior men to have been jettisoned is Mike Waltz, Trump’s first national security adviser, who was binned after less than four months, following his Signalgate mishap . (He ended up with a cushy consolation prize: ambassador to the United Nations.) A number of the discarded women had, shall we say, less than illustrious records

Zacharia—who failed the California bar yet repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer—was fired after five days on the job following a disastrous debut at the podium. (That’s less than half of a Full Scaramucci—the nickname for the 11-day tenure of Anthony Scaramucci, a fleeting supernova of a communications director during Trump’s first term.) Noem, meanwhile, presided over the killing of two Americans by immigration-enforcement officers in Minneapolis and spent taxpayer dollars on glitzy commercials, all while allegedly deferring to her rumored boyfriend, Corey Lewandowski (both have repeatedly denied an affair), to handle much of the Department of Homeland Security’s day-to-day operations

Bondi, for her part, seemed to view the top Justice post as that of Trump’s personal fixer. (Ironically, Trump’s ultimate frustration was not that she went too far in doing his bidding, but that she didn’t go far enough.) And Chavez-DeRemer, who left earlier this year, did so amid allegations of drinking on the job and an affair with a member of her security detail, as well as accusations from at least two female staff members that her husband had sexually assaulted them. (Chavez-DeRemer’s husband has denied the accusations through an attorney, and the police investigation of the reports has since been closed.) Like I said: These records are hard to defend

But even at the time of the Noem-Bondi double exit—Noem left in March, Bondi in April—a Trump official told me the administration risked the appearance of firing only “attractive” women , while allowing Trump’s top men to remain

It is not particularly difficult to list various sins and missteps involving many of Trump’s top male officials that, in most other administrations, would be grounds for serious reflection, if not outright dismissal

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—who had not managed an organization larger than about 100 before becoming the Pentagon chief—is the face and top cheerleader for the administration’s unpopular war in Iran, which helped doom Republicans’ midterm chances

FBI Director Kash Patel generated bad headlines for alleged misuse of an FBI jet, for a viral video of him chugging beers with the U.S. men’s hockey team at the Olympics in Milan, and for using FBI resources to ferry his girlfriend around the country

And few people in the administration seem to have anything good to say about Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whom they privately gripe about as Trump’s most annoying buddy and who has bungled trade negotiations and undercut the administration’s messaging on Jeffrey Epstein

Trump has stood by them all. [ Read: The king of queens ] “Donald Trump has demonstrated a much shorter fuse with women in power during the second administration,” Sarah Matthews, a deputy press secretary in Trump’s first administration, told me. “I’m not saying Kristi Noem and some of these women don’t deserve to be fired, but I think some of the men are not being held to the same standard

And it’s a pretty glaring disparity of who he’s willing to fire and who he’s not.” Matthews, who resigned after the January 6 attacks and now is a contributor at The Bulwark , said she blames misogyny, but also thinks that Trump often identifies with men under fire. (When Maine’s original Democratic Senate candidate faced allegations of sexual assault, including rape, Matthews noted, with a touch of exaggeration, that “Trump was the only person in America defending Graham Platner” before he dropped out.) Stephanie Grisham—a former White House communications director who also served as chief of staff to Melania Trump—recounted in a 2021 Washington Post op-ed that after she told Trump that her ex-boyfriend, a fellow White House staffer, had been physically abusive, the president expressed surprise
Neither he nor the first lady, whom she said she’d also told, ever followed up

Though Grisham did not name her alleged abuser in her essay, she was referring to Representative Max Miller of Ohio, who had become the president’s deputy campaign manager and kept his role despite Grisham’s disclosure to the first couple
Miller has since been accused of domestic violence by his now-ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and he lost his reelection bid last week

When I reached out to the White House for this story, the press office sent back a list of nine women whom Trump had elevated to senior positions, including Wiles (the first female chief of staff) and Leavitt (the youngest press secretary ever, as well as the first one to give birth while serving in the role)
An official also noted that Gabbard was neither fired nor forced to resign, but left because her husband was diagnosed with a rare form of bone cancer

In a statement, the White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers argued that the administration was a meritocracy, filled by people focused on delivering for the American people. “Unlike the identity-politics-obsessed Democrats, the President judges individuals on merit and qualifications, not immutable characteristics,” Rogers wrote

I also emailed the trio of women—Small Business Administration chief Kelly Loeffler, Education Secretary Linda McMahon, and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins—who remain in Trump’s Cabinet , to ask what they made of the high-profile-female departures, and see if they had any insights into why they had managed to survive for so long
The press offices of all three agencies wrote back

In a statement provided on her behalf, Rollins criticized “the constant effort to turn every personnel change into a gender story,” noting that Trump “has elevated women to some of the highest levels of government.” She added that, “as a woman, there is no one I would rather fight with to put Americans first than President Trump.” Andrew Nixon, the press secretary for the SBA, similarly said that Loeffler was proud to serve as one of Trump’s top officials. “President Trump hires based on talent and merit, not on gender, race, or any other social identity,” Nixon wrote

And the Department of Education spokesperson Ellen Keast wrote, simply, “ The Atlantic cannot even define what a woman is but has no issue extorting sexism for a headline.” Trump agencies are not always particularly responsive to reporter inquiries, but on this topic, all three were unusually prompt

After all, when you are one of a trio of women remaining in Trump’s Cabinet, it makes sense to be a happy warrior, relentlessly on message. *Illustration sources: Alex Wong / Getty; Kevin Dietsch / Getty; Eric Lee / Bloomberg / Getty; Eric Thayer / Getty; Samuel Corum / Sipa / Bloomberg / Getty; Alex Kent / Bloomberg / Getty; Jabin Botsford / The Washington Post / Getty; Getty.

title: Jensen Huang’s Apology May Be the Only Correct Use of AI
excerpt: Look, I just want to say that if Nvidia CEO and reported spy-plot target Jensen Huang did get help from AI to write an apology email to his family and company a
body: Look, I just want to say that if Nvidia CEO and reported spy-plot target Jensen Huang did get help from AI to write an apology email to his family and company about his affair (he’s said he uses AI to help write all of his first drafts), this might be the one use of AI that makes sense to me

People (me) are always saying about AI, “This is a solution looking for a problem!” and “Who would possibly want to delegate things like knowing information about your children or creating works of art to a third-party series of zeroes and ones?” But there are some things in life that nobody wants to do, such as get a root canal, amputate a limb, or deal with your cable provider

Or, perhaps, apologize simultaneously to your employees and your wife of 40 years for jeopardizing your business and personal relationships and perhaps also national security? (To me, though, those feel like two separate emails.) But I do see one problem for someone attempting to delegate the writing of this email: I don’t think this specific email has ever been written before, by anyone. “Business/Personal Email Apologizing for Affair/Possible National-Security Breach” is the email equivalent of those wedding dress codes—“Beach Formal”; “Back-of-Your-Closet Country Club”; “Cocktail Business Black Tie”—that are beyond what the human brain can understand
I’m just wondering what training data set one would even consult in this scenario
What template was AI going to work with here? James Bond scripts? (“I owe everyone here at Goldfinger Enterprises an apology

My fixation on James Bond and the time I have wasted designing a laser specifically targeted at his groin have distracted us from our mission of blowing up Fort Knox to increase the value of our gold supplies
To my many colleagues, especially Odd Job, I value our working relationship

Your dedication to throwing a sharp hat has not gone unnoticed, and you deserve better from me going forward.”) How many emails were in this data set? Were there, in fact, multiple emails from people apologizing to their families and employees simultaneously for potentially derailing the world economy over their relationship with a foreign spy that it could study? Is this a widespread problem? I understand that Donald Trump says of Huang that “he dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else,” but—I actually don’t think this situation is that common! I’ve never come across it in my life
Or if there is a spy trying to infiltrate my marriage to obtain my trade secrets (you will claw my log-in verification codes from my cold, dead hands), that spy is not very good at his or her job
But maybe I’m out of the loop! Maybe people just live like this

Now I am worried, based on Jensen Huang’s claim that this was “ completely normal and not unusual ” and an Nvidia spokesperson’s insistence that his interactions with the alleged spy were “ not unusual ” that, actually, we’ll be seeing multiple emails like this
Finally, organic demand for AI! If so, the template will get better and better—that is, if we can still use the chips.

title: Why Pete Hegseth Faces Impeachment
excerpt: Thomas Massie is pushing the House to impeach Pete Hegseth, the Cabinet member most closely associated with the Iran war
body: Thomas Massie is pushing the House to impeach Pete Hegseth, the Cabinet member most closely associated with the Iran war
The representative from Kentucky’s argument is that if Republicans like him don’t hold the secretary of defense accountable now for his various abuses of power, Democrats will in January
A vote in the House could come as soon as this evening
Massie, who was ousted by a Trump-backed primary opponent earlier this year, introduced his articles of impeachment against the defense secretary yesterday
It is Massie’s second attempt, following an unsuccessful effort in September
That time around, House Speaker Mike Johnson sent lawmakers home for recess instead of allowing a vote

Senator Ted Cruz said yesterday on his podcast that Johnson’s move was in part motivated by the fact that Republicans “didn’t have the votes to stop a Hegseth impeachment.” This time could end differently: Although most Republicans are likely to close ranks behind the GOP defense secretary in the middle of a war, only a few defections would create a majority for impeachment

The eight articles in Massie’s impeachment resolution focus primarily on four issues: the Iran war, the Pentagon’s campaign of boat strikes, Hegseth’s attempt to punish lawmakers for warning service members not to follow illegal orders, and the military operation in January to capture the Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro
In each case, Massie’s charges say that Hegseth either violated the law or engaged in disqualifying conduct while carrying out President Trump’s agenda
Congress has only ever impeached two Cabinet secretaries: Secretary of War William W
Belknap, in 1876, and President Biden’s homeland-security secretary, Alejandro Mayorkas, in 2024
The Senate did not convict in either case; conviction requires a two-thirds majority
Hegseth already looked likely to be the third Cabinet member ever to face the proceeding, now that a new Democratic majority will arrive in Congress in January

Hakeem Jeffries, the presumed next speaker of the House, said on the campaign trail that Democrats were ready to run the Pentagon chief “out of town.” Jeffries posted on Sunday that, when it comes to impeachment, he’s a “Hard Yes.” Other Democrats have also come out as enthusiastic backers

Pat Ryan, a former Army intelligence officer from New York, posted on social media that Hegseth “better buckle up and lawyer up.” Trump, meanwhile, has affirmed his support for Hegseth, telling reporters last week that he “has done a fantastic job.” Hegseth responded to the filing of the impeachment resolution at a Pentagon press conference today—his first in more than 180 days—arguing that any criticism of him was actually an attack on U.S. troops. “If they want to come for the warriors, they’re going to have to come through me,” he said. “What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability

It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.” The impeachment effort, Hegseth said, was intended to “do damage to this president, this country, and, most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it.” Hegseth added that every military operation mentioned in the Massie resolution had been approved by Trump, while emphasizing the president’s past impeachments and subsequent reelection. (Trump was impeached twice, in 2019 and 2021, by the Democratic-controlled House; although bipartisan majorities voted to convict him in the Senate, they fell short of the necessary two-thirds.) Trump responded to the press conference with a vote of confidence in Hegseth. “Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!,” he posted to social media minutes after the event wrapped

In a separate post last night, he described Hegseth as “perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country.” [ Read: Democrats are ready to run Hegseth ‘out of town’ ] Massie has used the prospect of an incoming Democratic majority to argue for a vote on his resolution now
His resolution, he said on social media, “is a much gentler version” of what may come
The House has two legislative days to act on the measure
Its options include proceeding to a floor vote by simple majority, voting to dismiss the resolution, or voting to refer it to a House committee to conduct hearings and gather additional evidence
Here’s what is in Massie’s articles of impeachment: Articles I, II, and III When the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran in late February, Trump didn’t consult Congress
Lawmakers had not authorized the strikes or approved a declaration of war
The War Powers Resolution, a law passed in 1973, allows the commander in chief to bypass congressional authority under limited circumstances largely related to self-defense
But early administration claims of an imminent threat from Iran quickly fell apart

Even in those cases where a president can act unilaterally, the president is required to terminate hostilities within 60 days or certify to Congress that conflict is unavoidable to gain an extension of up to 30 days

Its decision to go to war without congressional approval forms the basis of Massie’s first three reasons Hegseth should be impeached. (Hegseth maintained today that “history will judge the Iran war quite differently than conventional wisdom right now.”) Article IV The fourth article is also tied to Hegseth’s conduct in the Iran war, but includes a specific accusation: that Hegseth purposefully degraded the Department of Defense’s safeguards against killing civilians
In the first hours of the war, a U.S. strike killed about 170 people at a primary school in Minab; U.S. officials have said the tragedy was caused in part by outdated intelligence
Hegseth has dismantled offices at the Pentagon that helped the military protect civilians during combat
Staffing at the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, a Pentagon body created by law in 2023, was reduced by about 90 percent, our colleague Missy Ryan reported
Hegseth has called rules of engagement meant to limit accidental deaths “stupid” and advocated for the military to embody “maximum lethality, not tepid legality”—two quotes that Massie cites
Massie also suggested that the deterioration of journalistic oversight weakened the public’s understanding of harm to civilians

Hegseth imposed new, restrictive rules on the Pentagon press corps and expelled from the building journalists who wouldn’t comply. (These included staff writers at The Atlantic .) His actions eroded the Pentagon’s systems for limiting “collateral damage to civilians,” Massie wrote, and Hegseth “effected the murder of civilians and abused the trust of the men and women under his command.” At his press conference today, Hegseth said that “the only people who target civilians are the terrorists that we hunt, and I will dignify this claim no further.” Responding to criticism about the weakening of the Pentagon’s civilian-harm-mitigation efforts, a spokesperson had previously said that “the Department remains committed to minimizing civilian harm caused by military operations and to meeting all relevant statutory requirements.” [ Read: Why is the Pentagon afraid of the press? ] Article V Massie argues in this provision that Hegseth used the power of his office “in a manner that resulted in the extrajudicial killings of at least 243 persons aboard seagoing vessels alleged to be smuggling narcotics.” The military’s strikes on small boats off the coast of Latin America began in September 2025
The most recent strike, late last month, killed five people
The Trump administration has claimed that the strikes targeted boats transporting drugs for cartels
But officials have not presented evidence to substantiate that
Transporting drugs is not a capital offense under U.S. law

Hegseth “chilled independent legal review” in the Defense Department, Massie alleges, and relied on a “purported legal basis for the use of military force.” That refers to a memo from the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel that reportedly recasts cartel associates as legitimate targets in an “armed conflict.” (The memo has not been made public.) Many legal experts, including former military lawyers, have described the boat-strike campaign as a clear violation of both U.S. and international law
Nor does it appear to have achieved its stated purpose of reducing the flow of drugs into the U.S.; some evidence suggests that the flow of cocaine has actually increased over the past year

Hegseth has defended the campaign as part of an effort to secure “our Homeland from the drugs that are killing our people.” And the White House had told us previously that the boat strikes reflect how “President Trump is using every tool at his disposal to save lives from the scourge of illicit narcotics.” Article VI Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona appeared in a video in November 2025 along with five other Democratic members of Congress who had served in national-security roles before taking office

They reminded members of the military and the intelligence community of their obligation to “refuse illegal orders.” Their message was posted on social media after the Trump administration had deployed troops in several U.S. cities and conducted more than 20 lethal strikes in the drug-boats campaign

title: Trump Has Been Corroded by Hate
excerpt: “L et’s talk about death .” That’s what the 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat said to President Trump near the end of their interview that aired Sunday
body: “L et’s talk about death .” That’s what the 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat said to President Trump near the end of their interview that aired Sunday
Douthat asked Trump what he thought would happen to him when he dies. “I’m a religious person, so in theory I go to heaven,” the president said
When Douthat pressed him on whether he actually believes he’s going to heaven, Trump replied, “I hope so

I don’t want to go to hell.” Douthat then posed a hypothetical: “Let’s say you pass away, you’re entering the next life, and all you have to do to enter paradise is feel love and forgiveness for James Comey, Nancy Pelosi, anyone who you have expressed hate for over the years
Do you think you can do it?” Trump acknowledged that the easy answer would be, Oh, yes, I could forgive
He didn’t give it. “I found them to be extremely dishonest people, very bad people, very bad for our country,” he said
Pressed again, he was blunt: “The answer is no.” “Before the judgment throne of God?” Douthat asked
Trump didn’t budge. “No, I think they were very bad people and—I dislike, I can use the word hate , I do hate some of my enemies.” Moments later, he removed any doubt

Even before the judgment throne of God, with his eternal salvation at stake, would he forgive his enemies? “No, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.” N O POLITICIAN IN AMERICAN HISTORY has told as many lies as Trump
But on this question, I believe he was telling the truth
Jesus told his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them, and forgiveness is preached from American pulpits every week
But forgiveness is hard, really hard, and it’s especially hard to grant to those you believe have gravely wronged you. (In Trump’s case, he’s confusing being wronged with being held accountable

But he’s convinced himself that he’s been horribly mistreated.) [ Nick Clegg: Getting too close to Trump was a mistake ] Too many churches preach what I’d call “cheap forgiveness,” a cousin of what the theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer called “cheap grace.” Forgiveness takes time, and it should
Forgiving someone instantly usually means you haven’t yet reckoned with the pain
We have to make space to process the grief, anger, and trauma of suffering a deep injustice
That’s why “forgive and forget” is such bad advice
The Christian psychiatrist Curt Thompson argues that it gets things backward: Real forgiveness requires remembering
That means deliberately revisiting the hurt, ideally with others, until the memory is reshaped rather than suppressed
Cheap forgiveness is also a form of enabling
It lets the person who did the damage off the hook
When forgiveness comes too fast and with no cost, it can tell them that what they did wasn’t so bad after all
It lets them skip remorse, stunts their capacity for genuine empathy, and reinforces a sense of impunity
But Trump wasn’t simply acknowledging that forgiveness is hard
He seems to regard forgiveness as unnecessary at best and a sign of weakness at worst
For one thing, he has said he isn’t sure he’s ever asked God for forgiveness. “I don’t bring God into that picture,” he once explained

For another, he has turned the National Prayer Breakfast into a stage for denouncing his political opponents as “dishonest” and “corrupt.” He has preached vengeance at a gathering that, until Trump, had been a bipartisan refuge of reconciliation and generosity of spirit
B UT WHAT WAS MOST REVEALING about the 60 Minutes interview was how openly Trump owned the hatred at the core of who he is
He seemed almost proud of its depth and intensity
More than any other force, even his narcissism, hate seems to drive him
And it works on him like a drug: The more he indulges it, the more he craves it
Not even the deaths of men he considered enemies—John McCain, Rob Reiner, Robert Mueller—can satisfy his venom
When Mueller died in March, Trump’s response was, “Good, I’m glad he’s dead.” It has also crowded out joy
It’s hard to recall Trump ever seeming truly happy
And it leaves no room for intimacy, because anyone close to him might one day become an enemy
Hate often does its deepest damage to the one who carries it
In the end, it corrodes the soul of the hater
Trump’s hatred has also corroded the soul of his party
It’s striking how much the Republican Party—and how much of the Christian right—has come to resemble him during the Trump era
We see it in the brutal personal attacks, the proud displays of cruelty, and the delight in watching the strong hurt the weak

The party that for decades championed family values, law and order, and the formation of virtue and character in the young has become Castle Rock, Jack’s stronghold in William Golding’s Lord of the Flies

Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI —Grace Huckins As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI
Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy
I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor

But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.  “We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI

The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity  —James O’Donnell As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub
It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape
Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress
But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback
The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity

title: Evolving metal extraction processes
excerpt: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting
body: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible
Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago
Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize

Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations? EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted: “We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.” A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence

According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on
Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience
That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments

Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions
Beyond optimization For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control
EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways
The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production
Laboratory work revealed broader potential
Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions
They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed
The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness

Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology Source : Outokumpu Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world

Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT. “The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore
Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches

The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste

Innovation happens at the boundaries EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies
Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering

With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work. “Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn
Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production
Building a technology platform A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform
Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications
Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources
The initial application becomes only the starting point. “The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains
That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing
The future of materials companies The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy
Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives
The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027
The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030
Beyond producing low-CO 2 , chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum

The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today? The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on
Read more about this topic and hear more from Caspar Stinn and Antoine Allanore
It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

title: GLP-1 drugs carry risk of rare but serious eye condition – a physician studying these medicines explains the potential side effect
url:
<title>GLP-1 drugs carry risk of rare but serious eye condition – a physician studying these medicines explains the potential side effect</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771211/original/file-20261110-64-wbwdre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5358%2C3572&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Millions of people worldwide take GLP-1 medications.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/still-life-of-the-new-wegovy-semaglutide-tablets-with-out-news-photo/2258364671">Michael Siluk/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>GLP-1 drugs must now carry a warning label about a <a href="https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential">potential link to a rare eye condition</a> that can result in vision loss, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced on Nov. 9. 2026. The eye condition is called <a href="https://www.aao.org/eyenet/article/naion-diagnosis-and-management">non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy</a>, or NAION, and doctors often refer to it as a <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/5601-stroke">stroke</a> of the eye.</p>

<p>I am a <a href="https://ziyadalaly.com/">clinician and epidemiologist</a> who has studied GLP-1 drugs, and my colleagues and I published one of the studies that identified a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.9917">link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION</a>.</p>

<p>Millions of people around the world take these medications – including <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/712157/glp-usage-reaches-new-high.aspx">30 million in the U.S.</a> – to <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK551568/">treat diabetes and obesity</a> and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. They are being investigated for an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-024-03412-w">expanding list of clinical conditions</a>. </p>

<p>The data on which the FDA’s warning is based suggests a real but low risk of NAION for people taking GLP-1 medications. This is not a trivial or inconsequential outcome for those who develop the eye stroke. But on balance, if you’re using the medication for an FDA-approved condition such as diabetes or obesity on the advice of your doctor, the risk should not deter you from doing so.</p>

<p>Here’s what patients who use GLP-1 drugs need to know about this rare but serious side effect.</p>

<h2>What is NAION?</h2>

<p>NAION is an injury to the <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/22261-optic-nerve">optic nerve</a>, which is the nerve that connects the eye to the brain. This eye condition is caused by a sudden reduction in blood flow. Without enough blood flow, patients may experience sudden, painless blurry vision, dark patches, partial loss of vision or even blindness. </p>

<p>These symptoms generally persist and often lead to permanent visual impairment. Patients often notice these symptoms first thing in the morning when they wake up, as it tends to happen more frequently at night when blood pressure is naturally lower.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/fQVq8mtsVog?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">NAION, an injury to the optic nerve, can cause sudden loss of vision.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How did the FDA identify the connection?</h2>

<p>As use of GLP-1 drugs increased – particularly since <a href="https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/952441">2021, when they were approved for obesity</a> – cases of NAION began to emerge. A 2024 study of close to 17,000 patients referred to ophthalmology clinics was the first to show a potential link. It reported <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2024.2296">an increased risk of the eye condition</a> among the subset of those patients who were prescribed a GLP-1 drug. </p>

<p>To determine that the connection was strong enough to merit a warning, the <a href="https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential">FDA first compiled data</a> from 126 randomized, controlled clinical trials of GLP-1 drugs. Those trials included a total of 134,253 patients – 78,217 of them were on GLP-1 drugs and 56,036 received a placebo or a different medication, for comparison. </p>

<p>Per year, on average, the incidence of NAION cases was 6.4 per 100,000 people for patients taking the GLP-1 drugs and 3.8 per 100,000 among people given a placebo or other drug. This translated into 2.6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients on GLP-1 drugs.</p>

<p>In a separate analysis, the FDA reviewed GLP-1 drug data from its own network of <a href="https://www.fda.gov/safety/fdas-sentinel-initiative">sentinel programs</a> that track the real-world safety of approved medications. They assessed how often people with type 2 diabetes who started either a GLP-1 drug or two other common types of diabetes medications reported having NAION between 2019 and 2024.</p>

<p>Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a small but meaningfully higher risk compared to one type of diabetes drug, called DPP-4 inhibitors, which prevent the breakdown of the body’s own natural GLP-1. Over the course of one year, those taking GLP-1 drugs experienced NAION at a rate of 32 per 100,000 and those taking DPP-4 inhibitors at a rate of 26 per 100,000. This resulted in 6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients among people on GLP-1 drugs.</p>

<h2>Is there other evidence of the risk?</h2>

<p>Other studies that use real-world data such as electronic health records or insurance claims to track the health of people over many years have also found a consistent <a href="https://doi.org/10.2337/dc25-1238">association between GLP-1 drugs and NAION</a>. </p>

<p>For example, my colleagues and I tracked nearly <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.9917">600,000 U.S. veterans with type 2 diabetes</a> starting either a GLP-1 drug or a different drug over three years. For patients on GLP-1 drugs, we found that the incidence of this eye disorder was roughly 390 cases per 100,000 people, compared with 290 per 100,000 on an alternative medication. In other words, among people taking GLP-1 drugs, there were about 100 extra cases per 100,000 patients. </p>

<p>That number varied somewhat across studies, probably because of group differences among patients. For example, in some, patients were on average older, or also had other conditions that might contribute to their risk. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A schematic drawing of the anatomy of the human eye, including the optic nerve" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=528&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=528&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771214/original/file-20261110-64-bdx2pl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=528&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, is an injury to the optic nerve caused by a disruption in blood flow.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/human-eye-anatomy-diagram-in-flat-design-on-royalty-free-illustration/2156319135">Blueastro/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>What’s clear is that the slightly increased risk of NAION does not seem to be specific to any one GLP-1 drug but can occur regardless of which GLP-1 drug a patient takes. It’s possible that some GLP-1 drugs may have a higher risk than others, but so far, there’s no research addressing this.</p>

<p>The FDA’s announcement follows a 2025 review by European regulators, which examined NAION risk in only one type of GLP-1 drug, called semaglutide. It concluded that this eye condition is a <a href="https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/news/prac-concludes-eye-condition-naion-very-rare-side-effect-semaglutide-medicines-ozempic-rybelsus-wegovy">very rare side effect of semaglutide</a> and mandated that the package insert be updated to include NAION as a very rare side effect.</p>

<h2>The upshot for patients</h2>

<p>The risk of NAION with GLP-1 drugs is likely real. All the evidence – the FDA’s two analyses, the real-world studies conducted by independent researchers and the fact that two regulators reached the same view independently – points in the same direction. </p>

<p>But in terms of the total number of people who are likely to experience this side effect, the risk is small. In my view, this makes the FDA’s warning not a cause for alarm but rather an unlikely but not impossible outcome that both clinicians and patients should be aware of. </p>

<p>Clinicians should discuss it with their patients before prescribing a GLP-1 drug – and patients should be educated on the symptoms of NAION and how to tell if they are experiencing it.</p>

<p>Patients should also seek immediate care at the earliest signs of vision problems.  For patients who have previously had NAION or who already have <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2021.618353">risk factors for it</a>, including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, anemia and kidney disease, careful discussion weighing the risks and benefits is important.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296237/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Millions of people worldwide take GLP-1 medications
Michael Siluk/Universal Images Group via Getty Images GLP-1 drugs must now carry a warning label about a potential link to a rare eye condition that can result in vision loss, the U.S
Food and Drug Administration announced on Nov. 9. 2026
The eye condition is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy , or NAION, and doctors often refer to it as a stroke of the eye
I am a clinician and epidemiologist who has studied GLP-1 drugs, and my colleagues and I published one of the studies that identified a link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION
Millions of people around the world take these medications – including 30 million in the U.S. – to treat diabetes and obesity and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease
They are being investigated for an expanding list of clinical conditions
The data on which the FDA’s warning is based suggests a real but low risk of NAION for people taking GLP-1 medications
This is not a trivial or inconsequential outcome for those who develop the eye stroke
But on balance, if you’re using the medication for an FDA-approved condition such as diabetes or obesity on the advice of your doctor, the risk should not deter you from doing so
Here’s what patients who use GLP-1 drugs need to know about this rare but serious side effect
What is NAION? NAION is an injury to the optic nerve , which is the nerve that connects the eye to the brain
This eye condition is caused by a sudden reduction in blood flow
Without enough blood flow, patients may experience sudden, painless blurry vision, dark patches, partial loss of vision or even blindness
These symptoms generally persist and often lead to permanent visual impairment
Patients often notice these symptoms first thing in the morning when they wake up, as it tends to happen more frequently at night when blood pressure is naturally lower
NAION, an injury to the optic nerve, can cause sudden loss of vision
How did the FDA identify the connection? As use of GLP-1 drugs increased – particularly since 2021, when they were approved for obesity – cases of NAION began to emerge
A 2024 study of close to 17,000 patients referred to ophthalmology clinics was the first to show a potential link
It reported an increased risk of the eye condition among the subset of those patients who were prescribed a GLP-1 drug
To determine that the connection was strong enough to merit a warning, the FDA first compiled data from 126 randomized, controlled clinical trials of GLP-1 drugs
Those trials included a total of 134,253 patients – 78,217 of them were on GLP-1 drugs and 56,036 received a placebo or a different medication, for comparison
Per year, on average, the incidence of NAION cases was 6.4 per 100,000 people for patients taking the GLP-1 drugs and 3.8 per 100,000 among people given a placebo or other drug
This translated into 2.6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients on GLP-1 drugs
In a separate analysis, the FDA reviewed GLP-1 drug data from its own network of sentinel programs that track the real-world safety of approved medications
They assessed how often people with type 2 diabetes who started either a GLP-1 drug or two other common types of diabetes medications reported having NAION between 2019 and 2024
Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a small but meaningfully higher risk compared to one type of diabetes drug, called DPP-4 inhibitors, which prevent the breakdown of the body’s own natural GLP-1
Over the course of one year, those taking GLP-1 drugs experienced NAION at a rate of 32 per 100,000 and those taking DPP-4 inhibitors at a rate of 26 per 100,000
This resulted in 6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients among people on GLP-1 drugs

Is there other evidence of the risk? Other studies that use real-world data such as electronic health records or insurance claims to track the health of people over many years have also found a consistent association between GLP-1 drugs and NAION
For example, my colleagues and I tracked nearly 600,000 U.S. veterans with type 2 diabetes starting either a GLP-1 drug or a different drug over three years
For patients on GLP-1 drugs, we found that the incidence of this eye disorder was roughly 390 cases per 100,000 people, compared with 290 per 100,000 on an alternative medication
In other words, among people taking GLP-1 drugs, there were about 100 extra cases per 100,000 patients
That number varied somewhat across studies, probably because of group differences among patients
For example, in some, patients were on average older, or also had other conditions that might contribute to their risk
Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, is an injury to the optic nerve caused by a disruption in blood flow

Blueastro/iStock via Getty Images Plus What’s clear is that the slightly increased risk of NAION does not seem to be specific to any one GLP-1 drug but can occur regardless of which GLP-1 drug a patient takes
It’s possible that some GLP-1 drugs may have a higher risk than others, but so far, there’s no research addressing this
The FDA’s announcement follows a 2025 review by European regulators, which examined NAION risk in only one type of GLP-1 drug, called semaglutide
It concluded that this eye condition is a very rare side effect of semaglutide and mandated that the package insert be updated to include NAION as a very rare side effect

<title>Pa. Gov. Josh Shapiro’s popularity and ‘get sh-t done’ attitude might not cut it in crowded 2028 Democratic field – but he has options</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770381/original/file-20261105-64-kp8pjh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro arrives onstage to declare victory in his reelection bid on Nov. 3, 2026.

</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/democratic-gov-josh-shapiro-arrives-onstage-to-declare-news-photo/2302978410">Joe Lamberti via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/2026-midterm-elections-178375">2026 midterm elections</a> swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “<a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/massive-blue-wave-just-hit-053500218.html">massive</a>.”</p>

<p>In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection by 22 percentage points, <a href="https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/pennsylvania-governor-results/">winning more than 60% of the vote</a> – something that has been accomplished only <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_elections">twice before in the modern era</a> in the Keystone State.</p>

<p>Not only did Shapiro wipe the floor with his opponent Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer, but he also helped flip four U.S. House seats from red to blue. His coattails <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/09/campaign-finance-pennsylvania-governor-josh-shapiro-stacy-garrity-downballot-elections/">benefited down-ballot candidates</a>, helping Democrats solidify their control of the state House and <a href="https://theconversation.com/pennsylvania-democrats-now-have-power-to-push-forward-on-election-reform-marijuana-legalization-and-minimum-wage-increases-295731">flip the state Senate as well</a>.</p>

<p>Shapiro’s political stock in Pennsylvania is riding high.</p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://www.ship.edu/academics/cas/department-of-political-and-social-inquiry/faculty-and-staff-poli-sci/allison-dagnes-bio/">political science professor</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&amp;as_sdt=0%2C39&amp;q=alison+dagnes&amp;btnG=">political media researcher</a> in central Pennsylvania, and many of my former students work in Harrisburg. Some are Democrats working for or around the governor; others are Republicans working in different corners of state government. All are finely tuned to the political gossip that swirls around a successful politician whose star is on the rise. It is the worst-kept secret in American politics that Josh Shapiro wants to be president.</p>

<p>I’ve met the governor a handful of times and can attest to his George Clooney-level charisma. He’s a hard worker, has maintained a remarkably clean political profile, and is from many accounts a genuinely nice dude.</p>

<p>And yet, there are plenty of reasons his ambitions may require some careful timing, regardless of his personal strengths.</p>

<h2>A reputation for getting stuff done</h2>

<p>Shapiro’s political victories didn’t just happen. Over the past four years, he has worked <a href="https://theconversation.com/gov-josh-shapiro-has-a-reputation-for-getting-things-done-in-pennsylvania-but-not-necessarily-things-all-democrats-like-235854">to demonstrate bipartisan competence</a> as Pennsylvania’s chief executive, adopting an expression he uses frequently: “<a href="https://apnews.com/article/josh-shapiro-pennsylvania-swear-word-slogan-45db6d5d09a3a1e39bd13f4af70d1e23">get sh-t done</a>.”</p>

<p>Now, with Democrats holding the governor’s office and both chambers of the General Assembly, <a href="https://www.politico.com/newsletters/playbook/2026/11/04/after-the-flood-01148513">Shapiro told reporters</a>: “We got the power now, the House, the Senate. We have to deliver.” </p>

<p>Shapiro’s <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/30/josh-shapiro-pennsylvania-gubernatorial-race-2028-01137443">approval ratings have remained strong</a>, consistent with his reelection margins. That’s unusual in a state that has swung back and forth between supporting <a href="https://www.electionreturns.pa.gov/_ENR/General/SummaryResults?ElectionID=54&amp;ElectionType=G&amp;IsActive=0">Donald Trump in 2016</a>, <a href="https://www.electionreturns.pa.gov/_ENR/General/SummaryResults?ElectionID=83&amp;ElectionType=G&amp;IsActive=0">Joe Biden in 2020</a> and <a href="https://www.electionreturns.pa.gov/General/SummaryResults?ElectionID=105&amp;ElectionType=G&amp;IsActive=0">Trump again in 2024</a>, each time by fewer than 2 percentage points.</p>

<p>If Shapiro is indeed <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/5822245-josh-shapiro-2028-speculation-national-action-network/">seriously eyeing the White House</a>, his current popularity will certainly serve him well. But winning the presidency is an enormous undertaking, particularly in a crowded field.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Man in black T-shirt and black framed glasses holds a pint of Guinness and waves yellow rally towel in a bar" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770383/original/file-20261105-64-9qnpm3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Gov. Josh Shapiro tends bar and meets with constituents at a Pittsburgh Steelers watch party at the Cork Harbour Pub in Pittsburgh on Oct. 25, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/pennsylvania-democratic-gubernatorial-candidate-gov-josh-news-photo/2301535648">Jeff Swensen via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Stiff competition in 2028</h2>

<p>With Trump unable to run in 2028, the next presidential election will feature open seats for both parties and likely attract many candidates. Democrats, in particular, have a <a href="https://punchbowl.news/article/campaigns/dems-2028-campaign/">deep bench of attractive potential contenders</a>.</p>

<p>There are so many possibilities that Shapiro could find himself running against people very much like him: younger centrists, swing-state politicians and accomplished elected officials with solid records. Consider just a few names that could be part of the conversation: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel. </p>

<p>Shapiro would have to find a way to distinguish himself in a field filled with candidates who can make many of the same arguments about their experience, political appeal and accomplishments. That’s a tall order. A Plan B might be wise.</p>

<h2>Options beyond the White House</h2>

<p>Fortunately for Shapiro, other choices abound.</p>

<p>He could run for the Senate in 2028 against incumbent John Fetterman, <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/6208182-ahmed-moor-challenges-fetterman/">if Fetterman seeks reelection</a>. This would be a twofer: Shapiro would continue his rise in politics, and he would likely beat a guy he apparently does not like. The two <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/12/us/politics/john-fetterman-josh-shapiro-pennsylvania.html">reportedly don’t speak</a>, much less get along.</p>

<p>Shapiro could also position himself for a vice presidential nomination by attaching himself to another 2028 hopeful. This would buy him time to build his national profile, allow the presidential field to sort itself out and potentially put him in a strong position for another run at the White House down the road. It would also give him an opportunity to demonstrate that he can work effectively on a national stage.</p>

<p>Or he could angle for a Cabinet post. The federal government has undergone <a href="https://www.city-journal.org/article/doge-spending-cuts-civil-service-elon-musk">significant restructuring under DOGE</a> and Trump’s executive orders. Should a Democrat win the White House in 2028, rebuilding federal agencies and restoring institutional capacity will be a monumental undertaking. Shapiro could be an attractive candidate for a major administrative role.</p>

<p>The bottom line for Shapiro is that he will need to distinguish himself from a crowded field of Democrats by emphasizing his statewide victories in a major swing state, impressive fundraising ability and a political voice that <a href="https://www.tiktok.com/@msnow/video/7421241756592737579?_r=1&amp;refer=player_v1&amp;referer_video_id=7421241756592737579&amp;referrer">can evoke Barack Obama</a> without alienating either his party or the broader electorate. That’s a tricky feat, even for the most talented politicians.</p>

<p>But Nov. 3, 2026, showed us that he knows how to make sh-t happen. Whatever he decides, the next two years will be important for Shapiro, consequential for Democrats, and fascinating for political scientists like me, who will be watching events unfold with a keen eye and, probably, a bucket of popcorn.</p>
