<title>Students creating documentaries with scientists deepens STEM belonging and public trust in science</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769824/original/file-20261103-64-o22b4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4000%2C2666&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Communications and media studies student Evan Leong documents scientists breeding disease-resistant crops. </span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Ava Medberry</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Marine scientists navigate autonomous <a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/atlantic-crossing/">glider robots across the Atlantic Ocean</a> and along the <a href="https://beyondtheice.rutgers.edu/">West Antarctic Peninsula</a>, collecting data to help predict storm intensity.</p>

<p>When farmers’ fields are destroyed by an unknown pathogen, <a href="https://fieldsofdevotion.rutgers.edu/">plant scientists spend years</a> breeding new varieties of disease-resistant food crops. </p>

<p>A team of microbiologists <a href="https://mysteriesof9north.marine.rutgers.edu/">explore deep-sea volcanoes</a> in search of organisms that may contain anticancer compounds. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe src="https://player.vimeo.com/video/1239976215" width="500" height="281" frameborder="0" webkitallowfullscreen="" mozallowfullscreen="" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The science-in-action model teaches students to create documentaries that show the scientific research process.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>These are passionate people who are dedicated to seeking solutions to real-world problems. They are also the main characters in science documentaries produced in the <a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/">Rutgers Immersive Learning Science Storytelling Lab</a> that I oversee. Our lab pairs students with working scientists to co-create documentaries about research as it happens, while earning experiential learning credit.</p>

<p>At a time when <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/11/14/americans-trust-in-scientists-positive-views-of-science-continue-to-decline/">confidence in science is declining</a>, I was approached by scientists who wanted their authentic research stories communicated to broad audiences.</p>

<p>I am an educator, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=XRI_2kgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">a researcher and anthropologist</a>, and <a href="https://denaseidel.com/">a science filmmaker</a> who has been making science documentaries with Rutgers students and researchers since 2008. The science-in-action storytelling model I developed is intended to make the human journey of science visible to the public. Our stories communicate the process, motivations and integrity behind science, which <a href="https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10805-026-09732-5">helps earn public confidence and trust in science</a>.</p>

<p>I also partner with STEM learning researchers to gauge whether our documentaries increase the relatability of scientists, increase public understanding of scientific processes and help students find belonging in STEM.</p>

<h2>Our storytelling process</h2>

<p><a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/creation-process/">Science-in-action storytelling</a> is composed of five steps that support student-scientist relationships. </p>

<p>First, the storytellers develop trust with the participating university scientists. This trust stems from shared respect and a mutual understanding of the co-creation process. </p>

<p>The scientists then invite storytellers into their labs and field sites, where we capture their research processes in real time. This is Step 2.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Student recording a woman in a red dress on a beach boardwalk." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769135/original/file-20261029-64-yuho26.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Undergraduate philosophy major Ben Lerner was invited to accompany oceanographers to Barbados to make the documentary ‘Growing the Caribbean Glider Fleet.’</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Leah Hopson</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our professional storytelling team, which includes students, then documents scientists conducting research, including experiments and data collection, as they describe the why and how of their work. Depending on the complexity of the project, we collect dozens to hundreds of hours of science-in-action video footage. </p>

<p>Importantly, this video data is maintained in our storytelling lab, as it often includes recordings of federally funded research. Maintaining the video data repository is a key component to establishing and sustaining trust with the participating scientists.</p>

<p>Step 3 invites students to immerse themselves in the video data and begin shaping the footage into documentary scenes, constructed using only the scientists’ words, without narration. As they analyze hours of footage, our students learn about the authentic scientific processes; in doing so, they participate in research through the process of storytelling. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Young woman at a laptop editing film footage." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767319/original/file-20261020-50-5v0w6r.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Master’s student Shaniya Utamidata directs a 26-minute documentary called ‘Where the Waters Meet on the Breathing Shore,’ about scientists studying estuary biodiversity.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Dena K. Seidel</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our students are not graded on their documentary skills, nor are they required to make a film. Instead, they are graded on the science they learn through the storytelling process.</p>

<p>Step 4 requires that the students share drafts of their documentary scenes with the featured scientist to verify the accuracy of the science communicated. This step is part of the foundational trust agreement with the scientists but is also an opportunity for the students to personally connect with scientists.</p>

<p>For Step 5, our lab works to distribute the documentaries to a wide variety of audiences, including the general public. Here we partner with STEM learning experts to assess audiences’ understanding of and trust in the science communicated in the film and audience perceptions of the featured scientists.</p>

<h2>Reach far beyond the lab</h2>

<p>Our completed science-in-action documentaries have reached audiences far beyond the university. Our National Science Foundation-funded “<a href="https://beyondtheice.rutgers.edu/">Antarctic Edge: 70° South</a>” had a theatrical release and aired on Netflix. “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/atlantic-crossing/">Atlantic Crossing</a>” was broadcast on PBS stations and was included in a <a href="https://journals.ku.edu/jcel/article/view/22838/21753">three-year Smithsonian exhibit</a>. “<a href="https://fieldsofdevotion.rutgers.edu/watch/">Fields of Devotion</a>” was shared by the Association of American Universities as part of its <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NoYWvD6tAHw">campaign to increase public trust in science</a>. And our lab’s newest long-form documentary, “<a href="https://mysteriesof9north.marine.rutgers.edu/">Mysteries of 9° North</a>,” co-created with 14 undergraduates and featuring scientists studying life at deep-sea volcanoes, will be released to the public in early 2027.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Dozens of people sitting in the audience as students introduce a film screening." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=335&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=335&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=335&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767321/original/file-20261020-50-3sd4qs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Sean Feuer</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our surveys capture how these science documentaries change audience understanding of science and how it is done. For example, after screening “<a href="https://beyondtheice.rutgers.edu/">Antarctic Edge</a>,” viewers’ self-reported <a href="https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/communication/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2022.1049648/full">understanding of climate change rose from 71% to 91%</a>. On a 15-item knowledge quiz, average scores rose, with gains of up to 24 percentage points on the concepts they knew least about.</p>

<h2>Creating belonging for students in STEM</h2>

<p>When 102 undergraduates were asked what made the scientists in “<a href="https://fieldsofdevotion.rutgers.edu/watch/">Fields of Devotion</a>” relatable, they named passion for the subject (72%), desire to help others (71%) and commitment to their work (70%).</p>

<p>Our survey results also suggest that students who participated in the lab gained confidence and feelings of belonging in a science community. Undergraduates who once said they did not feel “smart enough” reported that <a href="https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/communication/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2022.1049648/full">they could now see themselves as scientists</a>. All participating students reported that their collaboration with scientists positively transformed their understanding of science. </p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">For the documentary ‘Amaranth: Cultivating Culture,’ undergraduate Zolani Kizito documents scientists as they analyze medicinal plant samples.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Dena K. Seidel</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Nonscience majors gained a deep understanding of the scientific process, while science majors gained rare access to research outside their own disciplines. </p>

<p>Student-directed science documentaries include “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/growing-the-caribbean-glider-fleet/">Growing the Caribbean Glider Fleet</a>,”  featuring scientists monitoring hurricane development; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/biting-back/">Biting Back: The Lifesaving Potential of Catnip</a>,” about the development of natural insect repellents; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/where-the-waters-meet-on-the-breathing-shore/">Where Waters Meet on the Breathing Shore</a>,” featuring climate scientists studying coastal ecosystems; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/the-b-a-s-i-l-project/">The B.A.S.I.L Project</a>,” about USDA-funded plant-breeding research; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/ocean-farming/">Ocean Farming</a>,” about NOAA supported oyster breeding; “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/the-women-of-nsongwe/">The Women of Nsongwe</a>,” about USAID-supported agriculture projects in Zambia; and “<a href="https://storytellinglab.rutgers.edu/skycatcher/">Skycatcher</a>,” about an NSF-funded atmospheric chemistry study in Alabama.</p>

<p>This science-in-action model offers a path forward that other universities could follow. Institutions can strengthen students’ STEM learning and science identities  while training a new generation of credible, relatable voices for science.</p>

<title>Democrats’ agenda will be set by their ability to organize and compromise — not by the socialist, progressive or centrist factions all claiming victory</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771116/original/file-20261110-78-ptg3b0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5500%2C3666&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Newly elected Democratic senators arrive for new member orientation meetings for the 120th Congress at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/senator-elect-annie-andrews-democrat-from-south-carolina-news-photo/2303880807?phrase=democrats%20congress&amp;adppopup=true">Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6022216/midterms-democrats-trump-republicans-analysis">massive Democratic majority</a> in the U.S. House and Senate that was ushered in by a <a href="https://www.rutgers.edu/news/what-drove-historic-blue-wave-2026-midterms">historic blue midterm vote</a> is an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/05/congress-midterms-diverse">ideologically diverse one</a>. </p>

<p>Candidates spent much of the past year differentiating their positions from the mainstream Democratic coalition. The result is a freshman class filled with as many <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2019/12/10/stephanie-murphy-moderate-progressive-freshman-democrats-080087">progressive liberals as moderate problem solvers</a>.</p>

<p>By the morning after Election Day, pundits and current Democratic members across the political spectrum were quick to claim their ideologically aligned candidates as the “<a href="https://prospect.org/2026/09/14/oct-2026-the-new-majority-makers/">majority makers</a>” – the group most responsible for the large victory.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.thirdway.org/memo/center-left-democrats-overperformed-and-delivered-the-majority">Centrist Democrats</a> pointed to pragmatic moderates flipping Trump-won seats. <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DoN2gy6oR5g">Liberal voices</a> highlighted the enthusiasm and turnout driven by a new, progressive vision.</p>

<p>As a result, days after the election the focus had turned toward January: Who will become the majority maker within Congress? </p>

<p>Party caucus leaders have already started <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/04/democrats-house-majority-agenda-01150963">building their roster</a>: The Progressive Caucus <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/09/progressives-us-house-flipped-seats">claims at least 25 new members</a> in their ranks, growing their membership to over 100 Democratic members. The moderate <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/04/democrats-house-majority-agenda-01150963">Blue Dog Caucus doubled in size</a>, from 10 to 20 new members. And in the middle, the center-left <a href="https://www.newdemactionfund.com/news/what-theyre-saying-new-dems-deliver-the-house-majority-and-prepare-to-lead">New Dems are projecting a caucus of over 140</a> members.</p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://sorellewg.com/">political scientist who has worked in and now studies Congress</a>. Figuring out the dynamics and direction of the 120th Congress requires looking at more than the ideological positions of the candidates who won. Instead, focusing on the number of candidates who won can provide insight into the direction of the party as a whole. </p>

<p>The large – and at the time of writing, still growing – margins of Democratic control in the 120th Congress are the <a href="https://www.caseyburgat.com/p/five-midterm-takeaways-with-pictures">biggest since 1993</a>, before Congress became consistently competitive and increasingly polarized. Those large margins provide essential context for understanding how this new ideological coalition will work in Congress.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771123/original/file-20261110-106-anyqzt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two men, one smiling and one speaking at a lectern, outside of a white building with columns." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771123/original/file-20261110-106-anyqzt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771123/original/file-20261110-106-anyqzt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771123/original/file-20261110-106-anyqzt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771123/original/file-20261110-106-anyqzt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771123/original/file-20261110-106-anyqzt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771123/original/file-20261110-106-anyqzt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771123/original/file-20261110-106-anyqzt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Sen. Chuck Schumer, left, and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, both of New York, are top candidates to lead congressional Democrats in their respective chambers.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/CongressDemocrats/46b73c1176f142b5932050a658a1461d/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=Schumer%20Jeffries&amp;currentItemNo=5&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photos/Mariam Zuhaib</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Size matters</h2>

<p>While history demonstrates that an <a href="https://theconversation.com/from-the-freedom-caucus-to-the-democratic-socialists-small-groups-inside-parties-can-wreak-havoc-with-leaders-agenda-in-congress-289362">ideologically diverse party can be hard to wrangle</a>, the size of the new Democratic majority provides some breathing room for policy negotiation and procedural debates. </p>

<p>Unlike the current Republican Caucus that is <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/12/17/slim-majorities-have-become-more-common-in-the-us-house-and-senate/">reliant on keeping historically narrow majorities together</a> to pass party goals, future Democratic leadership can stand to lose a few votes. With a minimum of <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Election_results,_2026:_U.S._Congress">254 seats in the House and 54 seats in the Senate</a>, small-scale Democratic defections are irrelevant.</p>

<p>This breathing room provides the potential for negotiation, while also limiting any mandate an ideological group may claim. </p>

<p>For instance, the 120th Congress will have eight members in the House who are <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/03/g-s1-150034/2026-midterm-election-dsa-candidates">backed or affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America</a>, known as the DSA. In raw terms of political power, when the majority has at least 36 votes to spare on any given party-line bill, this group may not matter in policymaking.</p>

<p>But big numbers do matter.</p>

<p>If a group – say, the entirety of the Progressive Caucus’ 100-plus membership – decides to stick together, leadership will be forced to listen. Thus, the potential power of ideological factions depends not only on their ideas but their own organizational skills. </p>

<p>When <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/D/bo249663334.html">groups in Congress develop practices</a> such as confidential meetings or binding rules that require members vote together on certain votes, the legitimacy of group demands can be strengthened. This is a strategy that has been employed with relative success <a href="https://theconversation.com/from-the-freedom-caucus-to-the-democratic-socialists-small-groups-inside-parties-can-wreak-havoc-with-leaders-agenda-in-congress-289362">by the far-right Republican Freedom Caucus</a> since it was formed in 2014.</p>

<h2>Details matter</h2>

<p>The overarching policy goals for newly elected Democrats are consistent across the ideological spectrum: lowering the cost of living and rooting out corruption. </p>

<p>This was highlighted in acceptance speeches by Democrats from <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gGe0WMQOx6I">South Carolina</a> to <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cK8wzjBpEoQ">Texas</a> to <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Btos5P_O2EY">Michigan</a>. All emphasized the same policy-focused promise: Instead of fighting left versus right, the fight should focus on the top versus the bottom.</p>

<p>This shared vision is no doubt important. My research has shown that a <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/E/bo280067639.html">cohesive message</a> is a key part of winning and maintaining majority control. </p>

<p>However, the “blue tsunami” was powered by voters with very specific policy demands. And as is always the case with policymaking, the details matter. Does healthcare reform mean reinstating the Obamacare subsidies set to expire on Jan. 1, 2027? Or does it mean something bolder, such as <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/3069">Medicare for All</a>?</p>

<p>While there is power in numbers, the organizational strength and ultimate success of ideological groups in Congress depends on how unified they can be around specific policy goals and proposals. </p>

<h2>First hurdle: Pick a leader</h2>

<p>This means that who is doing the unifying also matters. </p>

<p>The success of any potential legislative package heavily relies on congressional leaders’ knowledge of <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R42843">congressional rules</a> and their willingness to incorporate member viewpoints. </p>

<p>This necessity of having leadership in place to get legislation moving is epitomized by the order of operations for a new congressional session. In the coming weeks, <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/congress-returns-crowded-lame-duck-session-hegseth-impeachment/story?id=137918357">both parties will hold closed-door, secret-ballot elections</a> to <a href="https://www.house.gov/the-house-explained">select their new party leaders</a>. That’s well before any legislation is even drafted.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/DoN2gy6oR5g?wmode=transparent&amp;start=121" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A postelection interview with Texas Democratic Rep. Greg Casar, chair of the House Progressive Caucus, illuminates the horse-trading when a leader is chosen.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>With a Democratic caucus filled with anti-establishment candidates across the ideological spectrum, and external pressure from <a href="https://www.independent.co.uk/bulletin/culture/jon-stewart-chuck-schumer-midterms-b3080679.html">political pundits to dump current Democratic leadership</a>, the future of the Democratic Party has been <a href="https://apnews.com/article/democratic-future-2028-progressives-moderates-7890426d2bbd6bbc2c6f8b72e6f9a54f">projected onto this otherwise ritualistic vote</a>. </p>

<p>But the power and success of congressional leadership lies in its procedural acumen, not its ideological vision. <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DoN2gy6oR5g">Some already in Congress</a> have noted New York Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’ experience and working relationships in discussions of whether he should be house speaker. Furthermore, groups can extract concessions during leadership selection in exchange for their support, such as seats on powerful committees or an agreement on policy agenda items. </p>

<p>Sen. Chuck Schumer, the longtime New York lawmaker aiming to lead Senate Democrats again, <a href="https://edition.cnn.com/2026/11/07/politics/senate-democrats-new-majority-leader">faces more public criticism from his party</a>. While no one has yet stepped up as an alternative, momentum is building for <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6209487-van-hollen-senate-majority-leader/">Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen</a>, who has said he is “in listening mode.”</p>

<h2>Credit to all</h2>

<p>To external observers, the selection of party leadership seems like a defining point for the party. But whether a new caucus translates to new leaders or new rules ultimately depends on the organizational power of new members and their already-serving co-workers – and what a party leader can offer them in terms of policy goals and procedural capabilities. Who is chosen as leader is not necessarily a signal of what the party’s policy goals will be.</p>

<p>That picture is not yet clear – and it may not be for some time. After all, the new Democratic margins in Congress are a result of a collection of majority makers. The margins of victory tell a story about more than presidential backlash. Across the country, progressive enthusiasm and moderate appeal <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/04/us/elections/midterms-swing-voters-democrats.html">turned voters toward the Democratic Party</a>. And while everything is local, national enthusiasm matters, too.</p>

<p>The 120th Congress will include progressives and moderates and the establishment candidates in the middle that are all required parts of the same whole. Or as political scientist E.E. Schattschneider argued in 1960 in his seminal work “<a href="https://www.amazon.com/clp/0030133661?lv=shuf&amp;channelId=500">The Semisovereign People</a>,” it would be a mistake to give credit to one group for the success of an election. Rather, achieving a consequential majority in America requires coalition building – and maintenance.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296014/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>After midterm rout, Republicans can still confirm a Supreme Court justice, but at what cost?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771093/original/file-20261110-64-qxq2w3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5760%2C3840&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The Supreme Court is seen through a car window reflecting the U.S. Capitol dome on Nov. 9, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/APTOPIXCongress/b9e5c054c5c8492780c9f3e6b9a34166/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=Supreme%20Court%20US&amp;currentItemNo=8&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Allison Robbert</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://thehill.com/the-120/6209621-gop-midterm-loss-reckoning/">The 2026 midterm rout</a> that awarded Democrats <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-democrats-won-big-and-why-2028-remains-an-open-question/">decisive majorities in the Senate and House</a> has also sparked interest in <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/conservative-us-supreme-court-justices-thomas-alito-spotlight-after-democratic-2026-11-04/">the future of the U.S. Supreme Court</a>. </p>

<p>With Democrats securing at least a 54-seat majority in the Senate on <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RL30725">Jan. 3, 2027</a>, the window is rapidly closing for President Donald Trump to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/06/trump-rightwing-supreme-court-justice">appoint a new Supreme Court justice</a> and safeguard conservative dominance on the court for decades.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Kdr4x8oAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Supreme Court scholar</a>, I know that judicial appointments have real consequences. Look no further than <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1971/70-18">Roe v. Wade</a>: Within two years of securing a 6–3 conservative majority, the high court in 2022 eliminated the constitutional right to abortion that had existed for almost 50 years.</p>

<p>Now that Democrats have taken the Senate, if a Republican-appointed justice retires before Jan. 3, it will trigger one of the most explosive confirmation battles in American history.</p>

<p>Here’s how the fight is likely to play out – and why the stakes are so high.</p>

<h2>Who is most likely to retire?</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/democrats-dont-expect-fill-supreme-court-vacancy-trump-rcna600908">Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas</a> top <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/04/supreme-court-justice-alito-thought-about-retiring.html">the list of potential retirees</a> after Democrats won the Senate – even if Alito has reportedly said he <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/alito-trump-supreme-court-not-retiring.html">will not retire immediately</a>. Alito and Thomas are the court’s oldest justices, at 76 and 78, respectively. Thomas is the court’s longest-serving justice, appointed by President George H.W. Bush in 1991.</p>

<p>Perhaps more importantly, both justices have <a href="https://www.propublica.org/series/supreme-court-scotus">deep ties</a> to the <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-the-conservative-federalist-society-will-affect-the-supreme-court-for-decades-to-come-263397">conservative legal movement</a>. This is a network of lawyers, judges and politicians who seek to etch conservative principles into law. Overturning Roe v. Wade was at the top of the conservative <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-conservative-groups-will-advance-their-agendas-before-a-supreme-court-with-amy-coney-barrett-147084">wish list</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0329692">My research suggests</a> that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139626453">both Alito and Thomas care about their legacies</a>. And they both understand that a Democratic-controlled Senate will block another Trump-appointed nominee.</p>

<p>Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/6203353-chuck-schumer-donald-trump-supreme-court/">made this clear</a> just days after the midterms. And in October 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee member Richard Blumenthal, the <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/democrats-dont-expect-fill-supreme-court-vacancy-trump-rcna600908">Democrat from Connecticut</a>, said, “It is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration.”</p>

<p>Though Alito has indicated <a href="https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/10/06/congress/alito-retirement-lame-duck-01108410">he intends to stay on the court</a> through its 2026 term, Thomas has made no recent public statements about retirement. And Alito is free to change his mind at any time.</p>

<p>If Alito or Thomas announce their retirement soon, Republicans would have enough time to confirm a successor. The Senate has <a href="https://www.senate.gov/legislative/resources/pdf/2026_calendar.pdf">four and a half work weeks scheduled</a> between Election Day and Jan. 3. Justice Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12679">less than a month</a> after her nomination, making the timeline tight but doable.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman in a burgundy dress stands in front of a table and raises her right hand while several people wearing masks look on." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=361&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=361&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=361&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=453&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=453&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=453&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Amy Coney Barrett is sworn in during the Senate Judiciary Committee’s confirmation hearing for Supreme Court justice on Oct. 12, 2020, in Washington, D.C.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/supreme-court-justice-nominee-judge-amy-coney-barrett-news-photo/1229032886?phrase=Amy%20Coney%20Barrett%20confirmation&amp;adppopup=true">Shawn Thew-Pool/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Democrats will likely attempt to slow down the process, but they face an uphill battle with few options. <a href="https://time.com/4728558/neil-gorsuch-filibuster-senate-confirmation-vote/">Republicans stripped away key delaying tactics</a> in recent years by ending the filibuster in 2017 <a href="https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/press/rep/releases/senate-judiciary-committee-unanimously-sends-judge-barretts-nomination-to-the-full-senate">and ignoring</a> the <a href="https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/about/committee/rules">Judiciary Committee’s quorum rules</a> in 2020. This rule requires nine members be present to transact business, including two members of the minority party. </p>

<h2>A potentially historic battle</h2>

<p>A Republican effort to confirm a Supreme Court nominee during a lame-duck Senate would spark a historic battle with Democrats.</p>

<p>Democrats would surely point to how Republicans handled <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/president-obama-nominate-merrick-garland-supreme-court/story?id=37633715">President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland</a> in 2016. A seat on the court opened up <a href="https://www.npr.org/2016/02/13/140647230/justice-antonin-scalia-known-for-biting-dissents-dies-at-79">after conservative Antonin Scalia died</a> on Feb. 13, almost nine months before the November presidential election.</p>

<p>Republicans refused to move Garland’s nomination through the confirmation process, using their majority power to <a href="https://apnews.com/united-states-government-2d97d3c84cc445dc9e09a8406d901765">set the Senate’s agenda</a>. This marked the first time since 1866 that <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/history-stolen-supreme-court-seats-180962589/">a Supreme Court nomination that was not withdrawn</a> failed to receive an up-or-down vote in the Senate.</p>

<p>To justify this, Republicans created the so-called “<a href="https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/1464958/mitch-mcconnell-explains-his-rule-for-holding-supreme-court-vacancies-open/">McConnell Rule</a>,” named after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. According to <a href="https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/1464958/mitch-mcconnell-explains-his-rule-for-holding-supreme-court-vacancies-open/">McConnell</a>, the Senate should not fill Supreme Court vacancies “in the middle of a presidential election year.” </p>

<p>Four years later, Senate Republicans abruptly <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/27/us/mcconnell-barrett-confirmation.html">abandoned the rule</a>. This allowed them to push through Coney Barrett’s confirmation just days before the 2020 presidential election.</p>

<p>Democrats did not take kindly to this reversal.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765885/original/file-20261013-50-owyl5f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man speaks outdoors in front of a podium as people stand on steps in the background." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765885/original/file-20261013-50-owyl5f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765885/original/file-20261013-50-owyl5f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765885/original/file-20261013-50-owyl5f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765885/original/file-20261013-50-owyl5f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765885/original/file-20261013-50-owyl5f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765885/original/file-20261013-50-owyl5f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765885/original/file-20261013-50-owyl5f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer speaks in front of the U.S. Capitol after a boycott of the Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on the nomination of Judge Amy Coney Barrett to the U.S. Supreme Court on Oct. 22, 2020.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/minority-leader-sen-chuck-schumer-speaks-as-sen-dianne-news-photo/1281651759?phrase=Senate%20Minority%20Leader%20Chuck%20Schumer%20October%202020&amp;adppopup=true">Alex Wong/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Schumer pulled no punches in a speech the day of Barrett’s confirmation vote. Schumer <a href="https://www.democrats.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/schumer-floor-remarks-on-the-nomination-of-judge-amy-coney-barrett-to-the-united-states-supreme-court">said</a> the day “will go down as one of the darkest days in the 231-year history of the United States Senate.”</p>

<p>He alleged the Republican majority made “a mockery of its own stated principle – that the American people deserve a voice in the selection of Supreme Court Justices – completing the partisan theft of two seats on the Supreme Court using completely contradictory rationales.”</p>

<p>Democrats were clearly outraged by what they saw as two stolen Supreme Court seats.</p>

<p>However, I believe that pushing through a nominee will trigger an even fiercer fight. Senate Democrats will see such a confirmation as a power grab that sidelines the voice of voters.</p>

<p>Furthermore, if a Republican justice retires after the midterms, the move will almost certainly be viewed as purely partisan.</p>

<p>This has the potential to further <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.12820">erode public support</a> for <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/4732/supreme-court.aspx">the court</a>, which is sitting <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/07/30/favorable-views-of-supreme-court-remain-near-historic-low/">near historic lows</a>. And it will likely fuel the fire of Supreme Court reform, including the possibility of <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/supreme-court-reform-gathers-momentum">expanding the number of justices on the court</a>.</p>

<p>Put simply, in securing a short-term conservative victory, Republicans may end up handing Democrats the exact justification they need to reshape the high court.</p>

AP Photo/Allison Robbert The 2026 midterm rout that awarded Democrats decisive majorities in the Senate and House has also sparked interest in the future of the U.S

With Democrats securing at least a 54-seat majority in the Senate on Jan. 3, 2027 , the window is rapidly closing for President Donald Trump to appoint a new Supreme Court justice and safeguard conservative dominance on the court for decades
As a Supreme Court scholar , I know that judicial appointments have real consequences
Wade : Within two years of securing a 6–3 conservative majority, the high court in 2022 eliminated the constitutional right to abortion that had existed for almost 50 years
Now that Democrats have taken the Senate, if a Republican-appointed justice retires before Jan. 3, it will trigger one of the most explosive confirmation battles in American history
Here’s how the fight is likely to play out – and why the stakes are so high

Who is most likely to retire? Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas top the list of potential retirees after Democrats won the Senate – even if Alito has reportedly said he will not retire immediately
Alito and Thomas are the court’s oldest justices, at 76 and 78, respectively
Thomas is the court’s longest-serving justice, appointed by President George H.W
Perhaps more importantly, both justices have deep ties to the conservative legal movement
This is a network of lawyers, judges and politicians who seek to etch conservative principles into law
Wade was at the top of the conservative wish list
My research suggests that both Alito and Thomas care about their legacies
And they both understand that a Democratic-controlled Senate will block another Trump-appointed nominee
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer made this clear just days after the midterms

And in October 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee member Richard Blumenthal, the Democrat from Connecticut , said, “It is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration.” Though Alito has indicated he intends to stay on the court through its 2026 term, Thomas has made no recent public statements about retirement
And Alito is free to change his mind at any time
If Alito or Thomas announce their retirement soon, Republicans would have enough time to confirm a successor
The Senate has four and a half work weeks scheduled between Election Day and Jan. 3
Justice Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed less than a month after her nomination, making the timeline tight but doable
Amy Coney Barrett is sworn in during the Senate Judiciary Committee’s confirmation hearing for Supreme Court justice on Oct. 12, 2020, in Washington, D.C
Shawn Thew-Pool/Getty Images Democrats will likely attempt to slow down the process, but they face an uphill battle with few options
Republicans stripped away key delaying tactics in recent years by ending the filibuster in 2017 and ignoring the Judiciary Committee’s quorum rules in 2020
This rule requires nine members be present to transact business, including two members of the minority party
A potentially historic battle A Republican effort to confirm a Supreme Court nominee during a lame-duck Senate would spark a historic battle with Democrats
Democrats would surely point to how Republicans handled President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016
A seat on the court opened up after conservative Antonin Scalia died on Feb. 13, almost nine months before the November presidential election
Republicans refused to move Garland’s nomination through the confirmation process, using their majority power to set the Senate’s agenda
This marked the first time since 1866 that a Supreme Court nomination that was not withdrawn failed to receive an up-or-down vote in the Senate
To justify this, Republicans created the so-called “ McConnell Rule ,” named after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky
According to McConnell , the Senate should not fill Supreme Court vacancies “in the middle of a presidential election year.” Four years later, Senate Republicans abruptly abandoned the rule
This allowed them to push through Coney Barrett’s confirmation just days before the 2020 presidential election
Democrats did not take kindly to this reversal
Capitol after a boycott of the Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on the nomination of Judge Amy Coney Barrett to the U.S
Alex Wong/Getty Images Schumer pulled no punches in a speech the day of Barrett’s confirmation vote

Schumer said the day “will go down as one of the darkest days in the 231-year history of the United States Senate.” He alleged the Republican majority made “a mockery of its own stated principle – that the American people deserve a voice in the selection of Supreme Court Justices – completing the partisan theft of two seats on the Supreme Court using completely contradictory rationales.” Democrats were clearly outraged by what they saw as two stolen Supreme Court seats
However, I believe that pushing through a nominee will trigger an even fiercer fight
Senate Democrats will see such a confirmation as a power grab that sidelines the voice of voters
Furthermore, if a Republican justice retires after the midterms, the move will almost certainly be viewed as purely partisan

<title>US national debt keeps rising after years of tax cuts – and this will make policymaking all the more difficult</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770419/original/file-20261105-64-6q1iyh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C8%2C1992%2C1328&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A series of tax cuts since President George W. Bush&#39;s 2001 legislation have helped push the national debt to US$32 trillion.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/BUSH%20TAX%20CUTS/8e85b067ede6da11af9f0014c2589dfb/photo">AP Photo/Ron Edmonds</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Democrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/u-s-debt-just-topped-40-trillion-how-we-got-here-c1c6c9d2">national debt that now equals</a> the size of the U.S. economy.</p>

<p>Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/19/business/economy/us-debt-40-trillion.html">likely raise alarms</a> for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over <a href="https://theconversation.com/are-american-voters-actually-gloomy-about-the-economy-or-is-something-else-going-on-295476">the economy and the cost of living</a>. </p>

<p>Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been <a href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/tax-cuts-are-primarily-responsible-for-the-increasing-debt-ratio/">spending more than it collects in taxes</a>. Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt. </p>

<p>The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an <a href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/tax-cuts-are-primarily-responsible-for-the-increasing-debt-ratio/#f7">analysis of Congressional Budget Office data</a> by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found.</p>

<p>The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a <a href="https://www.du.edu/sites/default/files/2020-11/faculty_book_2020_FNL_pages.pdf">public policy scholar</a>, I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a <a href="https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c11009/c11009.pdf">relatively benign fiscal impact</a>. But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and <a href="https://theconversation.com/us-consumers-and-businesses-are-now-facing-a-future-of-more-expensive-borrowing-291848">interest rates are steeper</a>, the cost of adding new debt <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/pbaf.12386">is much greater</a> than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts.  </p>

<p>I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing. </p>

<h2>It’s all relative</h2>

<p>Proponents of <a href="https://atr.org/atr-backs-senate-commerces-a-i-moratorium/">fiscal austerity</a> argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise. </p>

<p>U.S. federal spending, however, <a href="https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/americas-finance-guide/federal-spending/#spending-trends-over-time-and-the-us-economy">has remained relatively flat</a> – outside of emergencies like the <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/111th-congress/house-bill/1/text">2009 recovery package</a> and <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/1319/text">COVID-19 stimulus funds</a> – even as <a href="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?g=20yTY">GDP</a> has risen. </p>

<p>At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a <a href="https://taxfoundation.org/blog/largest-tax-cuts-hikes-biden-trump-tax-proposals/">study by the Tax Foundation</a>, a nonpartisan think tank, noted.</p>

<p>President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, <a href="https://taxfoundation.org/blog/largest-tax-cuts-hikes-biden-trump-tax-proposals/">according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis</a>. The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth. </p>

<p>Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts. </p>

<h2>Costly extensions</h2>

<p>While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall <a href="https://www.jct.gov/getattachment/2f1d880c-ca26-429d-9044-63ac084d07cd/x-67-17-5053.pdf">10-year cost of $1.5 trillion</a>. That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025.</p>

<p>But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through <a href="https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/what-does-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-cost/">Trump’s legislation</a> that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts. </p>

<p>The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would <a href="https://www.cbo.gov/publication/61570">add another $3.4 trillion</a> over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to <a href="https://www.cbo.gov/publication/59710">116% of GDP by the end of 2034</a>. </p>

<p><iframe id="vjl3S" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/vjl3S/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Two side-by-side charts showing the growth in U.S. tax revenue and U.S. national debt since 1980."></iframe></p>

<h2>Why deficits and economic growth matter so much</h2>

<p>A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not.</p>

<p>If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, <a href="https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c11009/c11009.pdf">debt remains stable</a>. The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/u-s-debt-just-topped-40-trillion-how-we-got-here-c1c6c9d2">interest payments on government debt</a> are rising as well. </p>

<p>This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with <a href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/tax-cuts-are-primarily-responsible-for-the-increasing-debt-ratio/">lower tax revenue due to tax cuts</a>, the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office. </p>

<p>In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in <a href="https://www.thebalancemoney.com/us-deficit-by-year-3306306#toc-budget-deficit-by-year-since-1929">more tax revenue than it spent</a> and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats. </p>

<p>It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292099/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Hegseth escapes impeachment — for now
