body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth arrives to a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has narrowly escaped impeachment — for now.  What’s happening? On Tuesday evening, the House voted to refer an impeachment resolution against Hegseth to committee, functionally dooming it.  The vote, which fell along party lines with the exception of Republican Rep
Thomas Massie, who joined Democrats in voting against the referral, is a victory for Hegseth
The defense secretary’s future at the Pentagon has been under intense speculation since voters resoundingly repudiated President Donald Trump and the war with Iran in last week’s midterm elections
Prior to Tuesday’s vote, Hegseth had been facing impeachment as early as tomorrow on eight articles filed against him by Massie on Monday

Why did Massie want to impeach Hegseth? Broadly speaking, it’s because Hegseth is the public face of the extremely unpopular war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and he appeared vulnerable as even some Republicans voiced their dissatisfaction (though not, evidently, enough dissatisfaction for them to support impeachment).  Specifically, Massie charged Hegseth with: Waging war in Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution (three total charges);  Disregarding laws intended to minimize civilian casualties ;  Committing extrajudicial killings by carrying out missile strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific;  Suppressing free speech by trying to retaliate against Sen

Mark Kelly (D-AZ), a retired Navy captain, for a video by Kelly and other Democratic lawmakers reminding service members that they have a responsibility to refuse illegal orders;  Kidnapping former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife earlier this year; and  Waging an unlawful war in Yemen last year

What’s the big picture? Hegseth escaped, for now, with the support of Trump and Vice President JD Vance , as well as newly installed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.  But he could face another impeachment effort in the new year, with more than enough votes in the incoming Democratic House majority to see it pass (though not enough in the Senate for conviction and removal).  If that occurs, Hegseth will become the third Cabinet secretary in history to be impeached — and the second in less than three years
And with that, it’s time to log off… Vox’s Unexplainable podcast sat down with author Emily St
John Mandel (of Station Eleven fame) to talk about how she deploys science in her fiction

It’s a great conversation, and you can listen to it here .  Plus, a quick programming note: I’ll be off tomorrow for Veterans Day! One of my excellent colleagues will be standing in here, and I’ll be back Thursday

title: Hegseth’s “maximum lethality” comes back to haunt him
excerpt: Pete Hegseth speaks during a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026. | Pete Kiehart/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in Today,
body: Pete Hegseth speaks during a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026. | Pete Kiehart/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

In a matter of days, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could join a very exclusive club: Only two other Cabinet members have ever been impeached by the House…and one of them died 136 years ago.  Such impeachments are exceedingly rare because Congress generally treats them as a last resort — and because presidents can dismiss misbehaving officials themselves
But President Donald Trump has stuck by Hegseth through all his multitudinous misjudgments, from his cringe obsession with the Crusades to deadly strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean
Lawmakers will consider several of those alleged misdeeds when they vote on advancing Hegseth’s impeachment at 5:30 pm Eastern
The  articles of impeachment — filed by Rep

Thomas Massie, a Republican — specifically allege eight offenses, several of them related to the war in Iran and the fact that Congress never authorized it.  Hegseth is unlikely to be ousted, however, even if the House votes to impeach. (The Senate has a higher threshold for conviction, and it’s never removed a Cabinet secretary.)  But the Republican-led push to impeach Hegseth is still a striking rebuke of both the man and his uber-macho, unrepentant military philosophy
And that philosophy deserves our scrutiny, regardless of whether Hegseth keeps his job: It’s a matter of life or death

Go a little deeper Hegseth has dubbed his philosophy “maximum lethality,” and it’s more or less exactly what it sounds like: Military operations should deploy overwhelming force — to hell with “woke” distractions like civilian protections or legal oversight.  “No more politically correct and overbearing rules of engagement,” Hegseth said in a 45-minute lecture to senior military officials last year. “Just common sense, maximum lethality, and authority for war fighters.” Hegseth has been hashing out this doctrine of military maximalism for years — since his own time in the US Army National Guard
As the weekend co-host of Fox and Friends , he regularly defended service members accused of war crimes

He later published a book that argued progressive policies had ruined the military, titled The War on Warriors .  But even among “warriors” — Hegseth tellingly loves that word — this philosophy is pretty radical

Former military officers and legal experts say Hegseth’s dismissal of legal restraints breaks with generations of American military doctrine.  As early as the Civil War, the US propagated formal rules addressing the treatment of prisoners, the protection of civilians, and limits on violence in armed conflict. (“Military necessity does not admit of cruelty,” those rules read .) And decades later, the US helped prosecute Nazi war criminals at Nuremberg and shape the postwar Geneva Conventions
That’s not to say the US military has always practiced what it preached

But the US did at least preach restraint, whereas Hegseth has sought to make “rules of engagement” a dirty word on par with “DEI” and “climate change.”  He has championed flashy shows of overwhelming force, like the initial joint strikes that took out much of Iran’s leadership ; ordered strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean when a search and seizure arguably would have sufficed; and oversaw the capture of a foreign president , in his home, without congressional authorization.  Behind the scenes, Hegseth also cut funding and staffing for programs that mitigate and document civilian harm and fired the senior military lawyers who provide legal oversight to combat operations.  But Hegseth’s swaggering philosophy may be coming back to bite him
For one thing, overwhelming military force did not yield the decisive victory in Iran that Hegseth and Trump promised

For another thing, the phrase “maximum lethality” shows up several times in Massie’s articles of impeachment.  Massie is not, needless to say, a huge fan of the doctrine. “He has been effective, and that’s what we’re impeaching him for,” Massie said of Hegseth  on CNN . “His effectiveness in breaking the law and violating the Constitution.” One link for later ➨ Dabble in vegetarianism
Even if you’re familiar with the environmental and animal welfare benefits of forgoing meat, actually doing it can be hard
Or an abiding weakness for, say…a good kebab
Whatever your obstacle, it’s okay! Morally and practically, vegetarianism doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing proposition
Try giving up meat at certain meals or on specific days
Before you go… Did you know… that scientists estimate as many as 90% of the world’s species have yet to be discovered? There could be hundreds or even thousands of them in New York City , alone
Today’s trivia: What’s the name of the botanist supervillain in DC Comics’ Batman universe? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the animal that killed Cleopatra
That would be the asp, a type of venomous cobra, in many historical tellings — though many modern historians and toxicologists believe she committed suicide with a more conventional poison .

title: What to know about the Republican-led effort to impeach Pete Hegseth
excerpt: Thomas Massie (R-KY) speaks during a press conference on articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, outside the US Capitol in Washington
body: Thomas Massie (R-KY) speaks during a press conference on articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, outside the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on November 9, 2026. | Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth may be on track to become just the third Cabinet member in history to be impeached, after Republican Rep

Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against him on Monday.  Some articles of impeachment, which accuse Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors, focus on Hegseth’s conduct during the Iran war, including waging war without congressional authorization

Others accuse Hegseth of carrying out unlawful military strikes against boats carrying alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and the Pacific, suppressing free speech, kidnapping former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro , and waging unlawful war in Yemen
The articles are poised to move quickly in the House, with a procedural vote set for Tuesday evening and impeachment votes following as soon as Wednesday

Republicans still hold a slim House majority until January following last week’s Democratic tsunami in the midterm elections — but it’s possible that enough of them could join with Massie and House Democrats to impeach Hegseth anyway.  Hegseth, so far, has been defiant

On Tuesday, he defended his tenure atop the Pentagon in a rare press conference, calling the impeachment effort a “political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”  Following the press conference, President Donald Trump posted online that Hegseth deserves an “A PLUS PLUS PLUS” for defending himself

To figure out what awaits for Hegseth and what it could mean for the Iran war, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with the Washington Post’s Dan Lamothe about the impeachment effort, how the Pentagon is feeling after eight months of the Iran war, and whether there’s an off-ramp in sight
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify

What are the vibes in the Pentagon in Washington, DC? Did the Iran war lose Republicans these midterms? I don’t think it is the only deciding factor, but I think it is a significant factor in two ways.  One, there is a group of Republicans who voted for Donald Trump because he said he would not get us into any more protracted wars
The Iran war is eight months and counting
There seems to be no easy off-ramps even now

We’re certainly not at peace.  And as a result, the second issue — affordability, cost of living — a significant deciding factor in that is the price of gasoline, which then affects the price of groceries and everything else
So yes, there is a direct line between the war and a lot of the issues that were a factor
A lot of Democrats have been saying that they want to impeach Pete Hegseth if they take control
Future [House] Speaker Hakeem Jeffries came out this weekend and said that he’s into the idea
Remind us, why Hegseth?  I think there’s a couple of things going on
One, you’re likely to see an impeachment vote this week: the Rep
There are a lot of angry Democrats, obviously, but there are a number of Republicans likely to cross the aisle on this and it may very well pass the House
I don’t know if it’s going to pass the Senate
Either way, you’ve got an on-the-record rebuke, and you also have a forcing function to get every single member either on the record voting for it or on the record that they avoided voting for it
So that’s going to be a messy situation

What are the actual grounds for impeachment of Hegseth? On the Iran issue, it’s a little more complicated because you can think the policy of going into the war with Iran is problematic, detrimental to the national security of the country based on the amount of munitions we’re using, a variety of things

There’s not necessarily anything straight-up illegal in that.  Where I think they’re going to dig in is, they’re going to say that Iran went [on] longer than you’re allowed without having any kind of authorization.  Hegseth appears to be kicking off some sort of PR campaign in defense of his tenure
Is that just for the president or is that for Congress as well? I think it’s primarily for the president
I do think there is a secondary audience of members on the Hill — Republicans on the Hill in particular — who are not sure how to handle this going forward
But I think foremost, this was meant for the president
It was very Trump-esque in terms of its feel
It had a grievance in it and it had the feel of, they’re coming after me and I’m not going anywhere

I initially was like, this feels like that scene in Wolf of Wall Street where Leonardo DiCaprio says, “I’m not leaving.” And then within a day — I guess I should have seen it coming — the White House put out a video with a series of clips in it and sure enough, that was one of the clips

So that’s the vibe.  Even last week, when we saw Susie Wiles get pushed out at the White House as President Trump’s [new] chief of staff — Stephen Miller is much closer with Hegseth and you saw messaging from both sides, both the Pentagon and the White House, making the point that Hegseth continues to enjoy the support of both Stephen Miller and Donald Trump

And I think we’re all left wondering, does that continue into the new year with Democratic majorities in both chambers of the Congress at that point? How does it feel inside the Pentagon right now? What is the state of the war at this point? I think there’s exhaustion.  Not unlike some of the other earlier wars that we’ve covered, you go in with good intentions, you go in with a goal, there’s markers up on the board, there’s a campaign plan
And then at some point when it starts to go wrong, you can explain away some of the earlier problems
But the challenge is over time, when you say, “Hey, we won back in April,” and yet you still have vessels getting hit all the time.  The Strait of Hormuz, they say it’s open
There are still vessels getting through, but it’s under duress
There’s still missile fire coming at a lot of vessels
Everything is a drain.  There has been an increasing finger-pointing within the government, within the military where people say, “Hey, Hegseth is a participant in this

He’s a player in this.” There is at least a discussion of whether or not the president got the information he should have got, whether or not there was some gilding of the lily there in terms of what the US military could effectively do
And I think there are military officers there who are caught in the middle

Do you gussy it up on the front end or leave out some of the information that’s a little difficult for the president to digest in the first weeks of the war? And is that a factor on where we are now? Is anyone seriously talking about just ending this very unpopular quagmire situation of a war we’ve got in Iran? Certainly people are talking about it

title: Why the Nvidia spy scandal is so important
excerpt: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, pictured at the Invest in Germany Summit on October 19, 2026 in Berlin. | Thomas Koehler/Photothek via Getty Images This story appe
body: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, pictured at the Invest in Germany Summit on October 19, 2026 in Berlin. | Thomas Koehler/Photothek via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

The movie version of Jensen Huang’s jaw-dropping affair basically writes itself.  Cast BD Wong as 63-year-old Huang, the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies and a close friend of President Donald Trump

Kelly Hu can play Alice Huang, Jensen’s paramour and — even better — a purported agent of the Chinese government.  The role of Trump himself, who reportedly knew about Huang’s undercover girlfriend but on Sunday said Huang “probably has an excuse for it,” can be played by Alec Baldwin. (Or a flightless duck — your pick.) However you cast it, this whole sordid affair has “serialized Netflix drama” written all over it
But in all seriousness…the possibility that one of the world’s most powerful men was targeted by Chinese intelligence is a big deal on multiple scores
Nvidia has opened its own investigation into whether Huang was compromised, and congressional leaders have requested he brief them in a closed-door session

Nvidia supplies much of the computing power behind the AI boom, giving it enormous influence over the broader economy. “If they sneeze, everybody else catches a cold,” the writer and economic commentator Kyla Scanlon told Vox’s Today, Explained podcast last year
That makes this whole episode a little more weighty than your standard billionaire’s affair
Go a little deeper View Link Nvidia is the most valuable company on Earth — but in many households, it’s still not a household name

Huang and two other electrical engineers founded the now-$4.5-trillion company in 1993 with the fairly niche and nerdy goal of making high-powered chips that could render the 3D graphics for a new generation of video games.  Then, in 2006, the company released software tools that let programmers use its chips for other demanding computing tasks, like mining cryptocurrency and training AI models
When companies like OpenAI began developing tools like ChatGPT, they immediately turned to Nvidia.  That made the company a cornerstone of America’s AI buildout and a major economic force
In 2024, Nvidia alone accounted for more than a fifth of the S&P 500’s total return
And the rush to build out AI infrastructure has accounted for much of America’s recent economic growth , according to St
Nvidia’s influence  extends to the White House, too , where Huang is a regular guest of Trump

The two became fast friends after having dinner together at Mar-a-Lago last year, and Huang has said Trump regularly calls him late at night to discuss topics like “protecting national security” and “creating more jobs.”  But Huang’s ambitions have run up against one major obstacle: US restrictions on selling Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China
US officials worry that their enormous computing power could help Beijing develop weapons, strengthen its military, expand surveillance, and otherwise rival US military and technological dominance
That helps explain why China (allegedly) sicced a spy on Huang: They really want these chips

The New York Times reports that China’s top intelligence agency recruited Alice Huang both to learn more about America’s advanced chip industry and to potentially influence Nvidia’s push to lift export restrictions

Alice Huang, it should be noted, was a data center executive in her own right, and her company  has been investigated for purportedly helping to smuggle Nvidia chips into China.  All these investigations will hopefully, eventually, reveal whether their affair compromised anything beyond Huang’s marriage
They may also test how dependent Nvidia is on his leadership.  For now, Huang is staying on as CEO
But uncertainty over his future could unsettle investors and trigger wobbles in the wider market
That’s the problem with concentrating so much power in any one person or company: One person’s (very) personal business can somehow become everybody’s problem.  One link for later ➨ Get a hobby
But not just any hobby: something that’s intentionally imperfect, unproductive or unquantified
There’s a tendency in American culture to try to optimize or commodify our leisure , the writer Jenny Odell explains
But that undermines some of leisure’s biggest benefits — like cultivating a sense of joy, wonder, or learning
Before you go… Did you know… that Alexander Graham Bell reportedly wanted people to answer the phone with a cheerful “ahoy” ? Alas, Thomas Edison’s preferred greeting — “hello” — won out instead
Today’s trivia: Cleopatra was killed by what animal, according to several contemporaneous accounts? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for Ricky Martin’s biggest hit
That would be “ Livin’ La Vida Loca ,” the 1999 bop that’s widely credited with launching the Latin pop explosion of the late 1990s and early 2000s.

title: Robots could transform breast surgery forever
excerpt: “Wait, I can feel that?” Ami Brasure remembers thinking
body: “Wait, I can feel that?” Ami Brasure remembers thinking

For most of us, the experience that dazzled her couldn’t be more ordinary: You’re standing around, maybe in your kitchen or living room, drinking something a little too carelessly, and before you know it, the liquid is dribbling down your chin and trickling down your chest — and you can feel it
It’s a familiar sensation (in this case, perhaps an embarrassing one)

But for Brasure, a 50-year-old retail sales manager from the Washington, DC, area, it was life-affirming.  At the time, she was recovering from a double mastectomy in the wake of a stage one breast cancer diagnosis
She vividly remembers the chill from her spilled drink as it snaked its way inside the compression garment she was wearing as part of her recovery process

The sudden dampness came as a shock — not because it was unpleasant, but because she never expected to feel anything in that area at all, certainly not so soon after surgery.  Key takeaways Every year, hundreds of thousands of women in the United States are diagnosed with breast cancer and undergo mastectomies that can leave them with little to no feeling in their chests
In December 2025, the FDA cleared the da Vinci single-port surgical system for robot-assisted breast cancer surgery, specifically nipple-sparing mastectomies
Some surgeons are embracing this new technology because it offers a smaller, hidden scar and a clearer view inside the breast
Some patients also report better sensation in the chest area afterward

But critics say that there isn’t conclusive long-term evidence yet that robotic nipple-sparing mastectomies are as good as open mastectomies at making sure the cancer doesn’t come back, even if they are technically safe to perform
As Brasure knew, many people who get mastectomies are left with little to no feeling in their chests

That loss of sensation can affect a patient’s psychological well-being, sometimes actively alienating them from their bodies as they adjust to life after treatment.  “Every patient will have their own surgical goals
And mine was to look and feel as close as I did to how I looked and felt before I went into that operating room,” Brasure told me

Lucy De La Cruz, chief of breast surgery at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, offered Brasure the chance to be the hospital’s first patient to undergo a surgery that deployed a new robotic nipple-sparing mastectomy technique, she was enthusiastic

Especially because it was a procedure that some surgeons and studies have suggested leads to better preservation of feeling.  Using a robot to aid a mastectomy is not entirely novel — surgeons around the world have been experimenting with this technique for the past decade.  But what is new is that De La Cruz’s novel surgical plan combined several procedures into one operation
Using the da Vinci single-port robotic surgical system , she removed the breast tissue while preserving the nipples and skin
In the same operation, her team checked the lymph nodes, reconstructed the breasts with implants, and reconnected the nerve to the nipples to help restore sensation
In most robotic nipple-sparing mastectomies, the surgical incision is made along the armpit or the side of the chest
But here, De La Cruz and her team did everything through a single, 4-centimeter incision on each breast, naturally hidden under its fold
The hidden surgical scar and shorter recovery period, along with the possibility of having sensation back in her breasts post-surgery, were alluring for Brasure
Normally, surgeons performed nipple-sparing mastectomies through more conventional “open” techniques, typically through a long incision at the bottom of the breast
It is a technically challenging operation

Breast tissue extends all the way up to the collarbone, and surgeons have to reach it through a tight space with limited visibility, relying on their hands and eyes to look and feel their way around the breast

An assistant often uses large metal retractors to lift the skin around the incision to keep the area exposed and visible.  The procedure also carries a known risk of injury to the skin and nipple, sometimes severe enough that patients can lose the nipple and surrounding skin
These challenges led some surgeons to explore whether a robot-assisted surgery could help mitigate certain risks of open nipple-sparing mastectomies

But it was only in December 2025 that the Food and Drug Administration specifically cleared the use of the da Vinci single-port machine to perform mastectomies in the United States.  And at least for Brasure, it seems to have made all the difference, helping her feel better connected to her body after a procedure that might, under other circumstances, have left her with a radically altered sense of it
In theory, robotic nipple-sparing mastectomies sound like an amazing example of where surgical technology can take us
The American Cancer Society estimates that, in 2026, about 321,910 new cases of invasive breast cancer will be diagnosed in women

Many women opt for mastectomies not just as an active cancer treatment but also preventatively to reduce their risk, especially when they have a BRCA mutation — which indicates a very high likelihood of developing breast cancer — or a family history of the disease

A surgery with the potential to preserve more sensation, leave fewer surgical scars, and allow patients to recover more quickly promises to be a boon to women’s health.  Instead, robotic nipple-sparing mastectomies have proved extraordinarily divisive among oncological surgeons
Some, including De La Cruz, have embraced them
Others worry that the technology has gotten ahead of the evidence, especially on one of the most important measures in cancer treatment: making sure that the cancer doesn’t come back

The case for robotic mastectomies Maleeha Aziz, a 33-year-old deputy director at an abortion fund in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, grew up around breast cancer.  Aziz was 3 years old when her mother was first diagnosed

As a child, even though she couldn’t completely understand what was happening, she remembers her mother slowly losing her luscious, thick hair and how she could no longer pick Aziz up after the double mastectomy surgery.  It was clear that there was a family history, and Aziz felt like the cancer wasn’t skipping a single person
Her nani, or maternal grandmother, and her aunt had been diagnosed with ovarian and breast cancer, respectively

But the last straw was when her 32-year-old cousin — as close to her as a sister — received a stage three breast cancer diagnosis while she was pregnant.  Having seen the ravages of the disease firsthand and knowing from genetic testing in her early 20s that she was a BRCA carrier, Aziz ultimately decided that it would be better to get a preventative double mastectomy and reduce her cancer risk rather than live with pervasive anxiety from screening to screening.  “Preventative care is not radical
What is radical is to get cancer,” she told her family when they worried that it was an unnecessary medical intervention
A preventative mastectomy can lower the risk of breast cancer by close to 90 percent .  Aziz, like Brasure, was keen on sensation preservation

She remembered hating the numbness on her abdomen after her C-section delivery when she had her daughter, and couldn’t imagine the same around her breasts.  So in 2023, at the age of 29, Aziz opted for a preventative robotic nipple-sparing mastectomy at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center as part of surgical oncologist Dr
Deborah Farr’s study on the feasibility of using the da Vinci single-port machine to perform the procedure

title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here
As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub
It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape
Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ
It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves

Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words
But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes
I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits
The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity
There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite

In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.  One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy
Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables)
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts

That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .  Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity
Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair

But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.  Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else
Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand

Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand
The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way
The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to
Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines
Companies also build diesel generators for backup
Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company
Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded
The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts
It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts
That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out)
The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid

But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes
Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale
Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants
When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse

And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency)
Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around
Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do

But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers
Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think)
Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that

title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
excerpt: A new voice for AI regulation in Congress: Scott Wiener, who authored the country's first proposed frontier AI legislation, just won Nancy Pelosi's fo
body: A new voice for AI regulation in Congress: Scott Wiener, who authored the country's first proposed frontier AI legislation, just won Nancy Pelosi's former congressional seat and is already pushing for federal action — warning that "we could sleepwalk into a disaster." Recursive self-improvement is keeping him up at night: A recent report suggesting Anthropic may have achieved AI that meaningfully advances itself rattled Wiener, who sees it as proof that Congress is running out of time to act before losing control entirely

He wants regulation with real teeth: Wiener is pushing for a powerful federal AI regulator, whistleblower protections, kill switches, and auditing requirements — and he's firmly against federal laws that would strip states of their own ability to regulate

Cautious optimism, with caveats: Wiener is concerned about Congress's poor track record on tech regulation, wary of Trump's hostility to AI safety concerns, and hoping any crisis that forces action will be, as he puts it, "as small as possible." " data-chronoton-post-id="1148182" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI

Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.  I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor
But he was already thinking about AI risk

The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy

SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed

Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.  Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic

That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.  “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve

And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.  He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says

That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement
Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk
Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk
But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers

The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water

I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry

He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting
And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”
quotes: we could sleepwalk into a disaster.

title: The Download: empty AI climate claims, and an Nvidia investigation

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made —By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence
The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action
But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet
AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change
Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land

Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction.  The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree.  For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide.  Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate.  —Matthew Ponsford The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Nvidia is investigating its own boss Jensen Huang has admitted to intimacy with a suspected Chinese spy. ( The Guardian ) Quote of the day “Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life
My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust
I have fallen short of that responsibility.” —Jensen Huang apologizes to Nvidia employees for his affair with a suspected Chinese spy in a mass email sent yesterday, the Washington Post reports

One more thing STUART BRADFORD AI is coming for music, too AI models are marching into a creative field that is uniquely vulnerable to disruption: music.   AI-generated creative works—from orchestra performances to heavy metal—are poised to suffuse our lives more thoroughly than any other product of AI has done yet.  The songs are likely to blend into our streaming platforms, party and wedding playlists, soundtracks, and more, whether or not we notice who (or what) made them.  Here’s why AI is set to forever change how we make music.  —James O’Donnell We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. body: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market

For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance

Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams
Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work
Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments

But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively

By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers
These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability
Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle
Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step

Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands
Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient
The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology

I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys

title: Christians are now getting freaked out by Trump
excerpt: In his first sit-down interview since the midterm elections, President Donald Trump speaks with Ross Douthat in the Roosevelt Room at the White House. | CBS New
body: In his first sit-down interview since the midterm elections, President Donald Trump speaks with Ross Douthat in the Roosevelt Room at the White House. | CBS News via Getty Images Every week, millions of Christians gather to worship and remember the tenets of the faith: belief in God, in Jesus Christ as his son and their savior, and in the Holy Spirit
Many utter the words of the Lord’s Prayer each week, and in doing so, ask that God forgive our sins, as we forgive those who trespass against us

These are the ABCs of the Christian faith — and they should theoretically be an easy answer to offer if, like President Donald Trump, you’re asked what might happen when you die, and what you might do when Judgment Day comes

And yet, when asked last week by Ross Douthat on 60 Minutes where Trump thinks he’ll go when he dies — and if he could forgive his political enemies if his salvation depended on it — Trump was brutally honest. “Well, I’m a religious person, so in theory I go to heaven,” he said. “I hope so

I don’t want to go to hell.” Could he forgive opponents like former FBI Director James Comey and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi? “Well, then I wouldn’t be real, would I? I mean, if I said to you, sure, the easy answer to that is ‘Oh, yes, I could forgive,’” Trump told Douthat. “The answer is no

I want to be honest, no.” Even if God asked it? “Before the judgment, no,” he said. “I do hate some of my enemies…I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.” “I'm a religious person, so in theory I go to heaven,” President Trump says, discussing what he thinks happens after death. “I don't want to go to hell.” https://t.co/8o5y8hcqtY pic.twitter.com/5LexpK2jEP — 60 Minutes (@60Minutes) November 9, 2026 The statements shook many Christians who watched clips or heard him say this on CBS

Perhaps the most interesting reaction has come from the religious right, from evangelicals, Catholics, and other Christians who have long sided with the president over the last decade of MAGA.  They’ve long defended him, seeing him and his movement as a vehicle to spread the Christian gospel and win policy victories, like banning abortion, restricting IVF, and fighting back against the rising tide of social progressivism

But in the wake of stunning losses for Republicans in last week’s midterm elections, when Trump’s grip on the GOP seems most tenuous, another crack seems to have emerged in his alliance with the Christian right

And that’s because his answers essentially removed the plausible deniability of the argument that many Christians have used to justify their votes for Trump: that though an “ imperfect vessel ,” he was still a Christian, had received the gospel, and wants to be saved
His close ally, the evangelical pastor Franklin Graham, explained the importance of the question (but did not directly address Trump’s forgiveness response) in a post on X: “Heaven has borders
Heaven has unique and very strict entrance requirements

To enter Heaven, the Bible tells us that you must acknowledge your sins, turn from them in repentance, and receive Jesus Christ by faith.” Trump’s response to the question about heaven, though, showed no understanding of these requirements. “Religion can’t save you — only a relationship with the Savior, Jesus Christ, can save you,” Graham continued. “Do you have that assurance?”  In unambiguous terms, Trump basically said he doesn’t

Why conservative Christians are actually divided over Trump this time That someone like Graham, one of the most widely respected American evangelical leaders, would weigh in at all this time shows how serious the concerns are among conservative Christians

In previous moments this year, when Trump has similarly tested the religious right , it was easier to dismiss blasphemy, in part because it was directed at Catholics like Pope Leo XIV and his bishops (with whom politically conservative Catholics tend to have disagreements) , or could be dismissed as a joke — as when he shared AI art of himself as Jesus Christ
After strong backlash from evangelicals over that meme, he backed down and deleted the post

This time, the criticism is coming from all over — from theological conservatives like the Eastern Orthodox Rod Dreher , from evangelicals and other Christians , from Catholics — and that’s because there are multiple problematic layers to his most recent polemic

For the longest time, it was easier for Trump allies to say that though he was an imperfect sinner , Trump could still be saved , could still do good for their movement , or argue that he was still a Christian

But that’s much harder to do when he is failing multiple tests — including the most important one for evangelicals: having and declaring a personal relationship and belief in Jesus Christ is kind of the main thing , the key to being able to call yourself a Christian and have hope of being saved at the hour of judgment
Being “religious” doesn’t get you to heaven; being saved by grace through faith in Christ does

Graham summed it quickly when describing what it means to “receive Jesus Christ by faith”: “That means, believe that Jesus Christ is God’s Son, that He paid the penalty for your sins by dying on a cross, was buried in a tomb, raised to life on the third day, and walked out of that tomb.” I watched @CBS @60Minutes tonight, and Ross Douthat interviewed President @realDonaldTrump
Toward the end of the interview, they talked about something far more important than politics

He asked the President, at 80 years of age and after surviving multiple assassination… — Franklin Graham (@Franklin_Graham) November 9, 2026 That Trump was unable to say this to Douthat throws a wrench in one of the common defenses of the authenticity of Trump’s faith

And to some evangelicals, the fact Trump wasn’t able to say this was revelatory: a sign that none of the ministers, priests, pastors, or faithful who work for him have been able to convert his heart or help him be born-again

The evangelical theologian Al Mohler, the president of the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary, put it this way on his podcast on Monday: “It’s also very clear that [Trump] certainly needs to hear the gospel.” He continued to say that he will be “praying for him, with a renewed sense of urgency, that he has an experience of grace that he comes to know the Lord Jesus Christ as savior, that he knows the forgiveness of sins.” It’s that second point about forgiveness that got Trump in trouble with more Christians — forgiving your enemies, and praying for them, is one of the core tenets of the Christian faith, and of gospel teachings
Dreher also referenced this part in his X post when he referred to “the pettiness and hatred in that man’s heart
He is literally a character in Dante’s Inferno

Despite being given so much in life, he hates his enemies more than he fears God.” Now, none of this is to say that Trump has fully lost the Christian right — most of the evidence points to evangelical Christians and a collection of other Protestant, Mormon, and other Christians still backing him and the GOP in polling and elections, albeit by smaller shares than before
But for the first time in the decade-long Trump era, his hold on this movement is precarious
After appearing to compromise on a range of priorities for them , he and the GOP have suffered a once-in-a-generation loss
Trump is now digging into a nihilist, “ post-Christian ” identity, in Dreher’s words, demonstrating he is unrepentant even in defeat
This all puts the religious right in uncharted waters
Years ago, Douthat himself pondered what American politics and society might look like if the right gave up on God
Now, in the wake of political devastation for the right, he has presented a new question: What might the religious right look like if it gave up on Trump?

body: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said

body: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes

title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted

body: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994
High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party
